Self-adaptive, reliable software systems are crucial for avoiding crashes and ensuring successful operation in diverse environments. Nevertheless, the increasing reliance on real-time applications has made it challenging to ensure adaptive software adapts at the pace of its surroundings without disrupting its own functioning. This work addresses the need for a methodical approach to developing self-adaptive systems that can quickly respond to changes, maintain their integrity, and minimize performance loss. To this end, we have developed an adaptive processor-efficient algorithm for estimating a node's location and tracking its movement in a signal-intensive environment. To safeguard its reliability, the algorithm communicates with a backup processor, swapping data and incorporating corrective information from the secondary processor, thus ensuring continued operation even if the primary processor crashes. Our research uses a dual-core System-on-Chip, enabling seamless recovery and system continuity through a novel data transfer strategy between processors. This approach promotes a reliable, efficient self-adaptive technology framework, providing a theoretical foundation for developing robust software systems in the future. Our experiments show that the flow of data between processors has a negligible impact on localization accuracy and tracking precision.

The helicities of gauge bosons are typically considered to have standard, independent properties. However, when interacted with particles like fermions, certain combinations of helicities become accessible, potentially adhering to unique coupling rules rather than the standard model's predictions. By examining $W^{\pm}Z$ events resulting from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, accompanied by zero or one jet, in a dataset totaling 36 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the ATLAS detector, strict limits on anomalous gauge boson helicity combinations are imposed. These findings contradict the standard model's expectations, yielding the most restrictive constraints to date, with key parameters experiencing a 6-7% deviation in sensitivity, outperforming existing constraints at the CDF Tevatron and LHCb.

In our previous letter, we introduced a tensor called the Cotton tensor, appearing in 3D asymptotic 2D gravity. Its appearance can be generalized to higher dimensions as well. Additionally, its connection to the Einstein action in 3D gravity with a Chern-Simons term has been previously understood. Its generalized context in 3D gravity with a Chern-Simons term in any group has also been figured out. In this letter, we generalize the Cotton tensor to higher, specifically higher-central-charge theories in 3D in the Chern-Simons framework.

The concept of geometric duality applies to certain algebraic structures by relating isomorphic lattices in geometry to equivalent algebraic structures. This paper explores geometric duality for lattices with an orthogonal complement, a more complex algebraic structure. The study demonstrates that geometric duality for such lattices encompasses multiple cases, including distributive lattices with right or left complements. Furthermore, geometric duality for generalized Boolean algebras also falls under this broader category.

We introduce a visualization tool, coq-psv, that renders proofs from the Coq theorem prover into interactive structures, facilitating exploration and explanation. This can be particularly beneficial in making proofs more accessible to those without in-depth understanding of advanced mathematical concepts. coq-psv can be downloaded via OPAM or accessed online at coq-psv.inria.fr, supporting visualizations of up to 5000 steps due to performance constraints. A comprehensive demonstration is available through the coq-psv-in-education repository, showcasing its utility in educational settings for students learning to use the Coq theorem prover.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of Hecke maass forms can be bounded from above by $N^{4/2+1/4}\log N^{4}$, where $N$ represents the dimension of the space. This supplements Iwaniec and Sarnak's [Math. Ann. 308, No. 2, 167-211 (1994)] findings and offers a revised version of the result from Vinogradov [Sibirsk. Mat. Zh. 13, No. 1, 118-129 (2012); English translation in Russ. Math. Phys. 13, No. 1, 273-284 (2012)], who proved the analogue for holomorphic Hecke cusp forms with a certain growth rate. Our innovation lies in the introduction of a novel method for deriving non-uniform bounds on the Fourier coefficients of Maass forms.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, the inner iteration is often accelerated with multigrid or preconditioned Krylov solvers. The standard termination criterion for Krylov solvers in IPMs seeks an residual reduction below a specified threshold relative to the initial residual. This study investigates whether an alternative termination criterion, based on the interior point method's scaling parameters, could be more beneficial. The proposed criterion is proven to be more stringent than the standard one and ensures that the solution remains in the interior of the feasible region. Theoretical justifications demonstrate that this alternative criterion can lead to fewer iterations in IPMs. Moreover, the possibility of taking larger step sizes in the IPM algorithm is also explored. The suggested modifications are substantiated with numerical experiments involving a coupled system of two nonlinear equations, commonly encountered in multiparametric programming.

We have derived the polarized transition matrix (TM) components $A_{gq}^{(3)}$ 
for charm and bottom flavor pairs in QCD using an approach at order $\alpha_s^3$
based on the exclusive differential cross-section of jet production in polarized
epithermal proton proton collisions. The TM components were first expressed in a
composite (scale $\mu$) and simplified (heavy quark mass $m_q$) form, then applied 
to a beyond-next-to-leading order (BNLO) flavor QCD counting scheme in a numerical
analysis. The numerical results from TM value projections indicate a significant 
though expected increase in the charm and bottom flavor pair contributions in 
a BNLO accuracy compared to next-to-leading order (NLO) estimates. The charm and 
bottom flavor pair contributions in a BNLO accuracy are expected to be in line 
with each other. The numerical results from flavor pair momentum distributions 
validate the validity of the variable flavor counting (VFC) method at next-to-next-
to-leading order (NNLO). The charm and bottom flavor pair contributions in a 
BNLO accuracy are expected to significantly reduce the uncertainties in both 
inclusive jet production cross-sections and heavy quark masses.

In the journey of AI development, the path is littered with numerous mistakes that have led to severe consequences such as fatalities in self-driving car incidents and missile misdirections. These incidents could have been avoided or mitigated if previous errors had been learned from. We propose the AI Incident Repository, a knowledge base that documents AI incidents to prevent similar repeatability of errors. The repository's potential is showcased through case studies on how it could have prevented the mentioned self-driving car fatalities and a recent incident involving medical chatbot misdiagnosis. Additionally, the repository's implications on various AI topics, including transparency and accountability, are explored, and potential challenges and strategies for data collection are discussed.

We propose a new method of renormalization, applicable to a broad range of systems, which combines the principles of gradient flow and renormalization to eliminate the arbitrary aspects of the procedure. This technique can be employed to derive the renormalization group equation, which describes how the Lagrangian evolves at different scales. It also enables the calculation of the pole mass and beta functions with high precision. Our approach is outlined using a simple non-Abelian gauge theory as an example, but it can be applied to a wide range of quantum field theories, including the study of asymptotic safety in quantum general relativity.

This work presents an innovative approach for validating system behavior against dual process specifications, combining the benefits of both flow-oriented and task-oriented methodologies. By treating these specifications as regular language expressions, we can leverage acceptance conditions to define expected behaviors. However, dual process specifications introduce ambiguities, so we propose an extended monitoring system that incorporates conflict resolution strategies. Building on existing dual process monitoring research, our method adapts these strategies to use dispute management techniques, providing multiple options for resolving ambiguities. Moreover, system analysts can analyze the outcomes of these strategies, allowing for a comparative assessment of different approaches and ultimately, the selection of the most suitable technique based on performance metrics.

Quipper is an embedded domain-specific language for quantum circuit design embedded in Haskell. An earlier version, Proto-Quipper-M, was used in a recent study for evaluating quantum circuit design options. This paper presents a formal framework for static analysis based on continuing work from a previous study on quipper execution. The proposed framework expands on existing results by incorporating subcircuits, re-imagining quipper as a proto-quipper-m based on basic quantum operations, and adapting existing results to proto-quipper-m. The proposed framework results in a new definition for machine semantics with verified proof of relevance to quipper compilation. The key advantage of this approach is the ability to generalise quipber compilation to any embedded quantum circuit design language similar to quipper, with the existing compilation system already tested in multiple scenarios.

In recent years, particularly in information age, various forms of data have been generated, including large social networks, which necessitate the analysis of rare or exceptional events to prevent potential risks. Due to the limitations of conventional statistical methods in handling exceptional cases, researchers have turned to theoretical frameworks, specifically those based on stochastic matrix theory. However, existing methods often struggle to provide comprehensive results, especially regarding rare events, which this study seeks to address. By integrating techniques from both statistical physics and modern machine learning theory, the researchers developed a new method to study outliers in various systems. This method, which can be applied to both equilibrium and dynamic systems, has been validated through numerous applications, including the exploration of Twitter discussions during major events. The researchers discovered a universal scaling property in the main distribution and discussed the critical implications of this finding for detecting rare or exceptional cases in large network systems.

We suggest creating pairs of non-identical dipoole particles using a combination of optical experiments and measurements of long-lived dipoles linked to a cavity. A key aspect of this proposal is the relationship between two optical dipoles generated in a nonlinear optical system, where one dipole is in a highly focused laser field and interacts with a second, off-center dipole. We propose that this system, characterized by distinct dipoles, could be mirrored in a scenario where a long-lived state in a cavity-interacted system is measured, resulting in a pair of non-identical dipoles. We then explore the generation of pairs and the accumulation of squeezing in long-lived states, facilitated by rapid switching of light from a cavity, leading to a relationship between optical dipoles and long-lived states. This connection enables the assessment of optical phase through the measurement of non-identical dipoles.

Assembling long, uninterrupted DNA sequences from short reads using de novosolutions has become more efficient with the increasing storage capacity of modern computers. The time-consuming step of creating contigs, a key challenge in genome assembly, can be accelerated through parallel processing on multiple compute nodes. Despite existing parallel algorithms, creating contigs continues to be a significant bottleneck in genome assembly. To address this limitation, we have developed a new parallel algorithm that creates contigs using a graph approach, which takes advantage of a novel data structure allowing for random access to graph nodes. By efficiently managing the creation of contigs, our solution has resulted in substantial speed improvements, outperforming the current best-performed program by 3 to 4 times, while also accurately matching the output of the leading program for the human genome.

A novel logistic equation, representing a significant extension to established models, is introduced. It is based on a phenomenon observed in cellular biology where populations, initially resistant to change, eventually respond to changes in their environment. This phenomenon is represented by a piecewise linear dynamic system, which exhibits complex behavior, including the emergence of globally stable homoclinic orbits. The presence of fractal boundaries in the system's phase portrait is confirmed and the formation of chaotic attractors is investigated. When the parameters of the system are restricted to those found in nature, the focus shifts from global dynamics to the analysis of periodic solutions within specific regions of the phase portrait. In particular, conditions are identified under which the system exhibits multiple stable periodic solutions, allowing for the creation of novel, sustainable ecological models.

The concept of statistical depth has been employed to analyze the temporal or spatial information contained in temporal or spatial point patterns. While this approach has demonstrated efficacy, it still presents certain challenges. One major issue is that the depth of a point pattern depends on the direction of time or space, which can make the assessment of its center and margins more complicated. Another significant concern is that this approach assumes that all observations within the point pattern occur at the same interval, which may not always be the case. To address these limitations, we propose a new method that uses the Isometric Log-Change (ILC) transformation to create a depth measure for individual data points. The ILC transformation shares certain similarities with the Box-Cox family of power transformations, but it has a key difference in that it eliminates variance for smaller values. This new method can be applied to a wide range of distribution models, including those that are not variance-stable. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we provide empirical evidence from simulated experiments.

A quantum-doped epitaxial graphene device with a hybrid structure of graphene and Bi$_{120}$ has been created and studied. This unique material combination exploits graphene's interaction with the Bonner-Fisher state in the quantum spin system of Bi$_{120}$, which acts as a novel superconductor with an ultra-low superconducting gap of 0.30 meV. By using a quantum number of 0.5 in the local superconductor, we observed an on-shell gap opening in the graphene phonon spectrum at 0.35 meV, which serves as evidence of strong coupling between the two material components. Furthermore, we discovered signatures of Cooper pairing between graphene and Bi$_{120}$ electrons, which manifests as elliptical orbits in the graphene electron density around the Dirac points. These findings demonstrate that the device has an ideal hybrid structure, which is a crucial requirement for integrating superconducting and graphene technologies.

Researchers from the J-Ultron Paul team utilized the TUNTO facility's capabilities at TUNL for accurate measurements of atomic moments $M_0$ and $Q$ related to nuclear magnetic dipole moments in naturally occurring germanium isotopes near neutron number 40. Experimental results were gathered using the bent-crystal technique combined with a traditional method. The researchers found significant agreement between their results and theoretical predictions from large-scale shell-model computations performed by the N3S0 group. The findings provided significant enhancements to previously existing data, with the new data suggesting a previously undetermined magnetic dipole moment in the isotone $^{51}$Cu. The research used a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches to investigate interactions between valence electrons and those in the core, offering new insights into the complex internal relationships within the atoms.

Researchers have introduced an innovative isochronous mass spectrometry technique that utilizes the instantaneous ion optical properties of the fragment separator FRS, where the magnetic rigidity $\Brho$ is employed to eliminate the mass dependence. By leveraging this approach, which utilizes an on-line accelerator to isolate short-lived nuclei, researchers have successfully demonstrated the high-accuracy mass measurements of two exotic isotones, ${ }^{42}$Sc and ${ }^{42}$Ca, with experimental relative standard deviations of $3.9\times 10^{-10}$ and $2.6\times 10^{-10}$, respectively. These measurements, which were based on multiple cycles of data collection at the GSI facility with a maximum ion optical transmission of 7% and 12%, have yielded highly precise mass values for these nuclei. The development of this new approach has significantly expanded the scope of isochronous mass spectrometry, enabling researchers to efficiently measure the masses of individual nuclei, even those that are extremely short-lived.

The Flexible Standard Model Simulation Toolkit is an open-source abstraction layer for lattice field theory simulations of the Standard Model. It provides a flexible framework for implementing lattice field theory algorithms and simulating the quantum fluctuations associated with the gauge field. The FSMTK toolkit is heavily based on the deal.II library, which offers a wide range of high-level algorithms and data structures for solving complex mathematical problems on a lattice. This paper provides an overview of the FSMTK toolkit and is intended to serve as a guide for users who want to conduct lattice field theory simulations of the Standard Model using the Flexible Standard Model Simulation Toolkit.

This paper tackles the structured text identification (STI) challenge, an essential step in document analysis for extraction and recognition purposes, by leveraging a framework that favors preferred patterns. Our approach begins with a basic algorithm and a set of predefined templates, allowing for rapid identification of structured text within unstructured documents. A heuristic search mechanism is implemented to discover additional patterns in case of failed detections, using the pre-defined templates as a starting point to avoid exhaustive search. To enhance detection accuracy, we introduce a preference system that favors patterns from multiple aspects, including spatial, structural, and contextual cues. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a large dataset of business documents, outperforming alternative methods in terms of accuracy and processing efficiency.

The NA61/SHINE collaboration has developed an analysis of 2018 proton-silver interactions captured by the CERN SPS, specifically focusing on the creation of top quarks through the top-quark pair's production. By examining the top quark's decay into charged leptons and missing transverse momentum, the analysis identifies an isolated muon and neutrino events within a 1.5 TeV kinematic range. As a result, the detection represents the first generation-specific observation of a top quark signature in fixed-target experiments. With an analysis of the di-muon mass spectrum, the cross-section for top quark production in proton-silver interactions is determined, aligning with 11.8 million predicted Standard Model occurrences. This study utilizes a statistical approach, relying on frequentist and Bayesian methods, to validate the detection against a background of 0.97 (systematic uncertainty 0.37) expected occurrences in reality.

Interactive Vision-Anchored Language (IVAL) tasks, such as directing a camera based on written instructions, are complicated by the discrepancy between written text and actual scene context. To overcome this, we propose incorporating an additional parsing task that translates verbal commands into meaningful SQL code. This approach allows the model to generate more detailed and context-specific instructions. To differentiate between written text and actual scene context, the model must compare the two and consider factors like visual focus areas and written descriptions. This comparison is represented as a key-value framework, with the two distributions merged to guide SQL code generation. Our method was tested on a newly created dataset and demonstrated superior performance in generating precise SQL code that is in line with the scene context.

The ongoing LoTSS is a large-scale radio survey that recently released its initial data, which includes nearly 1.2 million individual radio sources across 25 square degrees of the sky. These sources exhibit a broad range of spectral characteristics, with about 15% exhibiting significant curvature. To better comprehend these findings, researchers employed a complex statistical model to analyze the data and assign spectral energy index values to numerous pseudo-galaxies. These pseudo-galaxies were then used to investigate various aspects of galaxy development across a broad range of stellar masses. To validate their approach, researchers compared their results with existing data from multiple sources, which reveals notable agreement in terms of spectral characteristics and Hubble sequence progress. Building on this success, researchers are exploring the potential for significant biases in LoTSS source classification, which could impact their understanding of galaxy evolution. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to utilize LoTSS data to study the on-scale cosmological behavior of galaxies using deep Hubble Sequence data, which is still in the pipeline.

This paper addresses the High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDRML) problem, which involves recovering ranks of critical variables in a multiple regression model containing many variables and factors. To solve this, we introduce an adaptive strategy to a recently-devised sifting method from the Variable Selection via Maximum Correlation field. The novel approach enhances the original method's efficiency by dynamically allocating sampling weights to both the candidate variable selection and regression processes. As a result, it significantly speeds up computational time, reducing it by at least eight times over the existing method. Thorough experiments with simulated and real-world data validate the method's high accuracy and efficiency. Notably, it outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in solving the HDRML problem.

Utilizing a modified Osorio approach, we investigate the second-order entropy change of a system in contact with a heat bath under an arbitrary driving force. Our analysis reveals that the system's second-order entropy change is a convex function of the driving force when the system's initial condition is closer to its equilibrium state. This convex property holds true for both weak-driving forces and rapid changes, which are primarily governed by the Osorio exponent. Additionally, we observe that the system's second-order entropy change is a positively spiked function of the driving force when the system's initial condition is further from its equilibrium state. This positively spiked behavior is characteristic of both slow drivings and strong forces, which are influenced by the Osorio exponent in conjunction with the Levy-stable nature of the system.

This study investigates the previously unexplored link between the tools used to tackle environmental challenges and the impact they have on the economy. A framework for classifying the environmental impact of computational technologies was developed, featuring a group of key performance indicators. Through a case study, solutions for two pressing environmental issues, urban heat islands and air pollution, were evaluated for their potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in cities. A previously unseen aspect of these problems was identified, specific thermal properties of the urban environment were found to influence the efficacy of some proposed solutions in mitigating the greenhouse effect. Our work lays the groundwork for a essential indicator of urban computational ecology.

Business process execution can be systematically tracked and recorded in the form of business transaction logs. Analyzing these logs allows for the discovery of processes by examining their creation sequences, thereby identifying operational patterns, exceptions, and areas for improvement. Due to the evolving nature of business processes, which can change in response to various factors, processes often deviate from their initially prescribed paths. As a result, there is a pressing need to investigate and develop methods for detecting infrequent transaction log patterns that can inform predictions, optimizations, and adaptations of business processes.

A novel approach to regulating mistakes in fluid dynamics is presented using a goal-oriented technique based on the weak formulation. This method controls errors associated with goal-oriented adaptations in optimization and sensitivity analysis contexts. It can be applied to fluid dynamics models that utilize a generalized Boussinesq model for complex systems. To illustrate the utility of this approach, we developed an efficient algorithm to solve the dual problem and derived efficient a posteriori error estimates for goal-oriented adaptations. Additionally, we utilized a Hele-Shaw lid drive cavity problem with heat source to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in the context of heated fluid flow. Compared to a standard Navier-Stokes model, the Boussinesq model revealed distinct differences in optimized velocity and temperature distributions.

Problems like Vertices Cover, Distinct Sums, and Sum of Products on Trees, which are all contained in a broader class called Multiplying and Adding Problems, exhibit a unique property where their efficient solutions can be encapsulated within a smaller subgraph of at most O(k^2) size, caused by the limited storage capacity of binary vectors. This characteristic holds true for vectors of length N, where the maximum value of N is tied to the square of the number of vertices in the graph. In the case of Vertices Cover, the subgraph can provide the exact cover, whereas for Distinct Sums and Sum of Products on Trees, the obtained vectors achieve near-optimal values, specifically within a factor of 3 of the minimum possible sum. These findings follow a broader pattern of kernelization for these kinds of problems, providing crucial insights into their complexities and classification.

This research explores how individuals form opinions about others when there's limited assurance available, a concept that's been recently introduced. We've developed a model to analyze a situation where people's opinions about each other are based on two factors: either they have undergone a reliable process or they have not. We've conducted both a theoretical examination and an empirical study. The results from both investigations demonstrate that when there's a shortage of assurance, people tend to think less positively about those who haven't gone through the assured process. Furthermore, we've discovered that in environments with a shortage of assurance, societal well-being is at its lowest. We've also pre-tested the model through an online survey and found the data to be in line with our predictions.

A level fuzzy set is a valuable tool that can be utilized to model potential defects in a black hole at the quantum level. Research has shown that a classical black hole, when subjected to L\"{o}wner emitters, exhibits a steadily increasing level fuzzy set that ultimately approaches a constant value. Similarly, an asymptotically level fuzzy black hole develops a steady, low-frequency tail. Building on these findings, our research focuses on the internal geometry of the asymptotically level fuzzy black hole. Using an advanced emerger, we find that the inner metric of this hole resembles the interior of a Michelson-Morley eternally static black hole. Furthermore, our results reveal that the level fuzzy set of the inner region undergoes a steady, outward contraction. Alongside its Asymptotically Level Fuzzy classification, this type of black hole can also be classified as an Asymptotically Constant Fuzzy (ACF) black hole.

Using a theoretical model, our study addresses the ongoing debate over the delay between transcription and RNA synthesis. Through simulations, we investigated how transcription rates, polymerase density, and RNA lengths affect dynamics. Notably, our results reveal both local and global lags in RNA production, influenced by different mechanisms. When multiple genes are transcribed far apart, their RNA production is delayed based on their distance, suggesting a causal link. Furthermore, our model shows that changes in lag are linked to altered transcription rates, indicating the impact of transcription speed on RNA production delays. By predicting the distribution of RNA lengths, our model selects between two theoretical models, validating the hydra head model which predicts longer RNA lengths based on transcription start sites.

Recent research on 64Ni with a null spin deformed band structure reveals that the band is composed of 8-8, 6-6, and 4-4 orbits. The goal of this study is to identify the underlying root configurations of these bands. The study also presents results on the form coexistence at null spin in 64Ni using the Wyld-type time-dependent shell-model. The results from a truncated shell-model calculation based on an effective interaction show that 64Ni has a band structure that consists of multiple orbits and can be described by a 8-8, 6-6, and 4-4 configuration. The study also presents results on the form coexistence at null spin in 64Ni using the Wyld-type time-dependent shell-model. The results from a truncated shell-model calculation based on an effective interaction and a monopole tensor interaction reveal details of temporary form coexistence and form competition in 64Ni. The study also presents results on the excitation strengths of the bands through an iterative solution of the TDBSE equation. The study compares the results with experimental data and other theoretical predictions, and the results from a truncated shell-model calculation and a Wyld-type time-dependent shell-model show good agreement with experimental data.

We examine various chiral N=1 supersymmetric theories in six dimensions, 
constructed from SL(n+1) or Sp(n+1) bundles with a specific orientation, 
and demonstrate that their dualities are influenced by four-dimensional 
chiral theories, such as the E7 bundle with a specific twist. To establish 
these connections, we first simplify the six-dimensional theories by 
isomorphically mapping them to four-dimensional models on a plane with 
three tubes, effectively reducing the order of the differential form. 
Next, we formulate a set of rules that allow six-dimensional theories 
to be mapped to their four-dimensional counterparts. Lastly, we apply 
these mapping rules to the case of an E7 bundle with a specific twist.

A linear complementary set of group codes consists of pairwise orthogonal codes with the same index. We establish a criterion for the existence of linear complementary sets of group codes within a finite principal ideal domain, and further demonstrate that such sets exhibit a unique, $z$-index property where the size of the codes is a factor of $z^2$.

In exact inference for graphical models, the Most Probable Explanation (MPE) is a key concept, with efficient but complex algorithms available. We introduce a faster and more straightforward method for calculating MPE in tree-decomposable graphical models, which has a lower time complexity than higher-order factorization algorithms. We also provide a simpler and more efficient method for finding MPE in models with limited optimization. Compared to standard methods, our approach reduces the memory required by one order of magnitude, while its runtime is roughly three times faster. These findings are backed by extensive experimental results.

In public settings, individuals often lie on their backs with valuable items such as phones and wallets within easy reach, making them vulnerable to theft. This research proposes a solution to protect these valuables from being stolen by pinpointing their location on the ground using a camera and the sound it emits from the item's position. We present an innovative audio-visual fusion approach, called ProneLoc, designed to accurately determine the lying position of an item. ProneLoc is comprised of a sound detection algorithm, a place identification system, and a corresponding image and sound fusion model that adapts to both cameras and microphones. We conducted an experiment with 15 subjects and collected the required audio and video data manually, then assessed ProneLoc's performance using various metrics and methods, such as confusion matrices and precision-recall curves. The results demonstrate that ProneLoc achieves an impressive 0.88 accuracy well above chance level 0.25, proving itself a effective system for locating lying items in a prone position.

One of the main methods to slow the movement of a particle is by manipulating the fluids around it, which might lead to different types of flow disruptions, either by significantly altering the particle's movement or by having a temporary, minimal effect. Researchers are interested in understanding how these disruptions, known as shear augmentation transitions, behave, particularly their variation in magnitude as the disturbance to the fluid increases. By using a theoretical approach, the authors have found a universal pattern in the variation of the disruptions, based on the change in the fluid's velocity, which applies across various types of flows and their respective physical systems. This discovery is crucial because it might lead to new methods to predict the best ways to manipulate the fluids to achieve significant changes in the particle's movement.

This study explores the dynamics of electricity consumption in Ghana, specifically during periods of power shortages. To achieve this, the paper utilizes hourly electricity usage data from the distribution sector, supplemented by time series of power outages from the Distribution Company's Customer Care Monitors system, as well as real-time data on the System Frequency from the Ghana Grid Code. The selected analytical period spans from March 2015 to March 2016. The study begins with an examination of the country's power supply challenges. This is followed by an analysis of electricity consumption patterns, before moving on to modeling the dynamics of electricity usage during periods of power shortages. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for policy makers and researchers seeking to inform their work with empirical data.

A study demonstrated that people are unaware of the polarization of web search results in the US. The study found that nearly three in five Americans have never heard of the term "echo chamber." To test this, participants were given a mock news article about a non-existent topic that reflected one of two extremes - liberal or conservative. The study showed that repeated searches on Google from browsers associated with either extreme resulted in a failure to discover opposing views. In contrast, people who performed searches while not signed in to a Google account were able to access a larger number of pertinent sources. The study's results revealed that people's inability to recognize the limitations of their own perspective may lead them to overlook relevant information.

In the 1990s, a method was created to translate flowchart diagrams into code, which caused a significant shift in the thinking of program synthesis. We are taking this approach even further by employing a more recent and powerful technique to generate code based on these diagrams. Our model, Graph Recognition Convolutional Neural Network (GRCNN), is a novel graph neural network that first recognizes patterns in the diagrams, then generates the corresponding code by predicting the next function call from the current program structure. By doing so, it is able to learn a program that is missing parts due to errors or omissions. We have tested our model on a dataset of randomly modified flowcharts and the results demonstrate its superiority over a more basic model in both its ability to recognise patterns in the diagrams (precision) and the quality of the generated code (program distance).

This text discusses several years of research focused on expanding the contractivity approach, originally developed in the context of the Lorenz model, to a broader class of climate models. It introduces the key concepts of probabilistic contraction theoretically and provides a concise overview of the results achieved in the associated study.

The development of ground-based telescopes with exceptional resolution has enabled researchers to observe the light produced by kilonovae ejecta with greater clarity, which has sparked significant interest in understanding the opacity of these events. The appearance of a kilonova is influenced by the properties of its ejecta, specifically the fine structure constant, outer shell electrons, and atomic fractions. The Os isoelectronic sequence is utilized in this study to investigate the opacity of a kilonova using the schedule of an Os isoelectronic satellite. The research involves valuing the relativistic atomic energy levels of Os isoelectronics, Au IV, with the Sirius 2.0 atomic structure program, which employs the B-Spline method to evaluate energy levels. The study shows that for low-resolution observations, the opacity of a Os isoelectronic sequence approximates that of a Fe core, which supports existing observations. Nonetheless, for high-resolution observations, the opacity of a Os isoelectronic sequence differs from that of a Fe core, which indicates that a more intricate atomic structure is necessary to accurately understand the high-resolution kilonova spectra. The research also indicates that a more intricate atomic structure of a Os isoelectronic sequence is required to comprehend the high-resolution spectra of a P-Process.

Radiologists examine CT scans primarily to identify non-acute conditions, such as tumors, chronic diseases, and abdominal organ abnormalities. The process becomes more efficient when the software automatically segments organs, including the gastrointestinal tract, as part of the image analysis. However, the segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract on CT scans is often imperfect due to its low contrast, partial volume effects, and the presence of gastrointestinal gases. As such, techniques used to automate its segmentation are often imperfect. The objective of this study was to assess the performance of different algorithms for segmenting the gastrointestinal tract on CT scans and to evaluate their reliability when used in different combinations. The researchers analyzed 1,000 CT scans from 125 patients by applying six, previously developed techniques in a blind evaluation. While the techniques used for automatically segmenting the stomach and small intestine demonstrated high accuracy when evaluated by the researchers, the combinations were less reliable and made the upper and lower parts of the gastrointestinal tract difficult to define. The accuracy of the combinations also varied significantly, suggesting that these techniques are of limited clinical use. The feasibility of using these algorithms in clinical practice is also called into question by their poor reproducibility when used by different researchers and on different patient datasets. The techniques showed potential, but further refinement is required before they can accurately and reliably define the upper and lower parts of the gastrointestinal tract.

Compositional data can be represented as parts of whole entities, making up 100% of the entire thing. Examples include populations, chemicals in substances, or literary genres in collections. Analyzing this type of data poses unique challenges, primarily the scaling of variables and the lack of a clear zero point. We'll examine the mathematical underpinnings of linear models, coefficient interpretation, and visualization methods for compositional data. Our focus will be on the direct method of calculating coefficients and the common coefficients approach, both based on ordinal coordinate systems. We'll also explore the effective coefficients, a novel method that utilizes Simpson's identity, and the relationships between these methods and the log-ratio analysis. Our statistical findings will be applied to a hypothetical dataset, and real-world datasets will be used to illustrate the steps in the compositional data analysis process, from data preparation to the interpretation of results in the context of the research question.

Previous studies have suggested that a certain mass range, known as the desert region, in which exoplanets are less common, exists for Jupiter-mass planets with close orbital distances to their stars. However, these findings were primarily based on observations of a small, biased sample of stars with bright objects near the CORALIE/HARPS planetary search program target list. This program, which utilizes the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity dataset, aimed to investigate the existence of this 'desert' around 82 stars with observed properties similar to those of the initial discovery stars. By analyzing the program's results, no evidence could be found to support the existence of this 'desert' around the program's targets. Instead, a comprehensive linear relationship was discovered that explains the observed distribution of planetary masses and orbital distances in the sample. The program's results also indicate that the characteristic mass range of this 'desert' may be higher for planets with closer orbital distances to their stars.

To address the issue of model overconfidence in multi-modal datasets, we develop a new technique called Mutually Regulated Attention (MRA), which adjusts the behavior of Attention Mechanisms to reflect the distribution of class labels. A novel method utilizing Mutual Knowledge Enhancement is also introduced to simultaneously optimize both Attention Mechanisms and Traditional Networks. This regulator, utilizing drop-out information, facilitates a shift from task-specific to class-balanced attention patterns, thus preventing overconfidence. This regulator can be easily adapted to support additional features for Attention Mechanisms. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in regulating Attention Mechanisms and improving model performance.

To explore the lower mass range of compressed baryonic matter, consider a model involving a Yukawa interaction between $u$, $d$, and $s$ quarks and an unknown number of additional quarks with similar mass. For simplicity's sake, assume that these additional quarks do not participate in the formation of hadrons. Then, using lattice QCD data and magnetic properties as a guide, construct compressed baryonic matter composed of $u$, $d$, and $s$ quarks, introducing a new quark to stabilize it against decay. For instance, adding a single heavy quark with mass around 2 GeV to a compressed baryonic matter with mass around 3 GeV, consisting of three $u$, $d$, and $s$ quarks, yields a compact object with size around 10 km, where the strong and electromagnetic forces balance, at a density roughly 5-6 orders of magnitude higher than normal matter. In this scenario, the new quark can be thought of as a new type of baryon, where the forces mediating its interaction with ordinary matter, such as a dark photon force, play a crucial role in its stability. To explore its potential presence, an intense beam of protons or electrons could be directed at a compact object with properties similar to a neutron star, where its internal structure can be inferred from the object's disintegration or continued survival, using reactions that involve the creation of a dark photon or other

Our research shows that the simple Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can be
efficacious for a variety of cognitive tasks by introducing a novel
architectural pattern, where an RNN is connected to a utility layer only
after its output has been processed through a transformation. This
simplification leads to less complex learning for multiple cognitive
tasks, including learning in multi-step contexts, navigating in complex
environments and identifying complex patterns in data. Additionally,
our results indicate that the utility layer can be utilized to interpret the
utility of outputs by reversing its direction. By applying this pattern
to a sparsely-connected microcircuit model inspired by brain anatomy,
our study demonstrates that an artificial system can solve various
cognitive tasks more efficiently with less computational overhead.

We provide an exhaustive classification of transformation semigroups along with their corresponding nilpotent algebras based on the size of their bases, and offer a geometric interpretation of this classification through the lens of posets.

The emergence of Active Galactic Nuclei, specifically those with relativistic jets, is thought to occur when the black hole at the nucleus overwhelms the surrounding disc energy output. A recent study has explored how radiation from the cosmic microwave background affects the growth of these black holes and the strength of their jets in the most distant universes. Utilizing advanced cosmological simulations, researchers found that the impact of CMB on the accretion process is relatively minor compared to its influence on jet formation. Focusing on quasi-stellar objects, which are a type of AGN with relativistic jets, the study discovered that the CMB's shadow could reduce the number of jets visible in optical light from about 30% to 10% below a certain threshold of black hole mass. However, it's possible that in X-ray and infrared light, the frequency of these objects might increase by as much as 100 times.

We've identified two distinct Lagrangians that describe classical gravity in higher
spacetime dimensions, one of which generalizes the Einstein-Hilbert action and the other
is an alternative that arises from the variational bicomplex of the gravitational gauge theory}.
The first Lagrangian combines the Einstein-Hilbert term with a volume contribution proportional
to the square of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, resulting in a variational principle that remains
intrinsic to the manifold. In contrast, the second Lagrangian requires a cocycle from the de Rham cohomology
to form the closed 2-form, and it reduces to the Einstein-Hilbert action in four dimensions.
Both Lagrangians exhibit variational stability. Additionally, we find that the second Lagrangian
has a simpler mathematical structure and is associated with a more extensive group of symmetries.

This study presents a novel approach to establishing a point-set correspondence between two grayscale volumetric images, utilizing a combination of two techniques. Firstly, 3D SIFT is employed to create a correspondence between local volumetric features. Secondly, to refine and prune the correspondence, we propose using spatial symmetry properties, dividing the feature space into discrete, equally-sized bins along each dimension. As a result, each bin is assigned a score based on the symmetry score, ranging from 0 (no symmetry) to 8 (full symmetry), taking the form of $\mathcal{O}^{8}_{k} \cdot \mathcal{M}^{8}_{k} \cdot \mathcal{N}^{8}_{k}$, where $\mathcal{O}$, $\mathcal{M}$, and $\mathcal{N}$ represent the possible orientations, mirror reflections, and needle deformations of the feature, all of which contribute to the feature's desirability for registration. To extract features, we utilize a non-linear, sparse coding approach, utilizing the symmetry scores to filter and refine the feature space, ultimately leading to the establishment of a precise correspondence between the two image volumes. This correspondence is then utilized to generate registrations in both rigid and affine domains. Our approach is validated by experiments involving synthetic and real-world data, as well as comparisons with related methods.

We conducted a detailed analysis of the long-period binary star system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, known for its extremely short white dwarf and brown dwarf companion age difference. The team used photometry and spectroscopy to study the low-frequency fluctuations in the system's light, confirming it has low-amplitude, multi-band fluctuations at a 0.003 magnitude amplitude, with frequencies ranging from 0 to 0.317 cy/cy and lacking any visible signs of flaring. The researchers also confirmed a new low-amplitude orbital frequency of 1.092 cy/cy associated with the long-period (0.081 days) eclipses of the double-degenerate binary star system, the highest ever reported for such a system. The photometry results indicate the low surface mass fraction of material from the secondary star to the primary star is around 0.0006. The study also reveals that the photosphere of the primary star extends to a certain radius due to external pressure from a circumstellar envelope, with an estimated radius one per cent larger than its equilibrium value. The researchers also found that the system's long-period eclipses have irregular shapes and phases, likely due to changing accretion rates from the secondary star to the primary star, as well as other system components, such as a surrounding gaseous disk. The team observed that the time it takes for the primary star to complete an orbit has decreased by 0.000006 days, possibly due to gravitational

This study reinterprets global aggregation in terms of a special case of optimal transport, focusing on the behavior of aggregation methods when initial data varies. It presents a detailed analysis of the average error produced by global aggregation on a domain with a convex shape and demonstrates the negative effects of noise on the error for all methods, except in one specific instance where the error remains constant. This study offers a thorough understanding of global aggregation in the presence of noise and highlights its limitations.

The orientation of active galactic nuclei, particularly in relation to their host galaxies, holds significant information about their intrinsic properties. To gain a deeper understanding, researchers have made distinctions between different types of active galaxies, which, interestingly, also reflect themselves in the alignment of their host galaxies. By visually classifying over 8032 galaxies including 307 with an active nucleus, researchers used technique such as wavelet morphological analysis to understand their structural properties. The findings of a previous study indicated a relationship between active galaxy types and their host galaxy alignment. Building on this, the current research aims to examine this relationship in more detail, investigate possible differences between various active galaxy types and their corresponding host galaxy alignments. To this end, the researchers applied various statistical tests to compare the distributions of different active galaxy types and their corresponding host galaxy alignments. The results of these tests revealed no significant differences between the most numerous active galaxy type, that of the narrow line emission, and other types in relation to their host galaxy alignment. However, significant differences were found between the less numerous but more luminous broad line emission active galaxies and two less luminous types, that of the broad line emission and the composite line emission. The findings of this research, obtained through the analysis of a relatively large and diverse set of active galaxy types, are consistent with the current theoretical models.

Researchers find a unique flat surface in a 4D curved space that maintains its flatness under rotation for all points in space. A specific point on this surface has a distinct geometric property, which is analyzed using a specialized graph to determine its behavior under rotation. As a result, the surface can be divided into separate regions based on how they rotate and exhibit unique geometric patterns. Using a specific mathematical function, the structure of the rotating surface can be controlled and customized for any given rotation. Additionally, the study expands on a previously established theorem in the context of more complex 5D and 6D spaces.

A recent study revealed that deep neural networks trained on large, publicly available image datasets can achieve remarkable accuracy when applied to semantic segmentation tasks. However, the study also highlighted the limitations of using existing datasets for neural network pre-training due to inconsistencies in their annotations. To address these issues, this research investigates the effects of training deep models on a vast, publicly available dataset annotated with depth information, rather than the standard RGB information used in most similar studies. By doing so, the study aims to leverage depth cues to improve the robustness and accuracy of subsequent semantic segmentation tasks, even when depth information is not available in the test data. From a practical standpoint, having a neural network that can utilize depth cues to achieve high semantic segmentation accuracy is highly desirable. Moreover, many real-world applications rely heavily on depth information, rendered from monocular videos or or photos, making this approach even more relevant. By assessing various training objectives, the study demonstrates that training on depth-embedded datasets indeed leads to superior performance in semantic segmentation tasks, both with and without depth information. Notably, the study finds that training on depth information alone is sufficient to achieve high accuracy in semantic segmentation tasks that do not utilize depth information. This finding is attributed to the more widespread presence of depth-related cues in natural videos and photos. By contrast, training on more traditionally structured image datasets was found to be less effective in achieving high accuracy in semantic segmentation tasks.
