The contributors share their approaches to defining states using natural language for tasks like state observation, object interaction, and conversation reasoning, as well as discussing key challenges and promising areas for future research.

Our research focuses on determining the mass distribution of dark matter in a typical quasar using deep learning, which is represented by a convolutional neural network. By constructing artificial profiles with a predetermined level of noise, we simulated diverse systems of mass and radiation to train a model. By feeding only the radiation data into the model, we found that it can accurately predict the system's mass distribution. When evaluating on a dataset with a wide range of masses, our model achieved a strong correlation with the underlying mass spectrum, at or near a 1 in 100 likelihood. Additionally, we discovered that the model's performance is less dependent on the level of noise as it progresses further along the spectrum. This research is the initial step in utilizing machine learning for understanding the distribution of dark matter using broadband radiation. Due to the abundance of data from both the galaxy distribution and radiation, this problem is well-suited for machine learning. Once a model is established, it will enable the mass distribution of dark matter to be determined from quasar spectra, which are significantly easier and less expensive to obtain. This will significantly expand our knowledge of dark matter, particularly in areas that are difficult or too far away to be studied through galaxy redshift observations. Our findings have implications for numerous theoretical models, including halo biasing theories. Furthermore, we observed that the model's performance could be enhanced by utilizing spectra from an narrower wavelength range. This research may have far-reaching implications for understanding the dark matter distribution, particularly in areas that are difficult

For a finitely generated algebra $R$ over a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\frak h$, the authors determine classes of modules over the Lie algebra of derivation operators, excluding those represented by $\frak D_8$ and $\frak D_{8}(k)$ in specific scenarios, using the properties of a $U(\frak h)$-excluded module. Furthermore, the authors provide examples and implications for the Excluded Module Problem in the context of finite-dimensional Lie algebras of derivation operators.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become a necessity for making informed decisions.
In this paper, we present our solution to Twitter sentiment analysis, which won first place at
the Data Science Cup 2021, by leveraging various techniques. Our objective, given a word
sequence consisting of annotated tweets, was to predict whether the sentiment was positive,
negative or neutral. Our final model, an LSTM-based framework with dropout, outperformed
other contenders by achieving a test accuracy of 85.29%, along with a remarkable 0.236
error rate, also earning us the top spot in the competition.

Recently, large-scale language models have shown exceptional open-domain
conversation abilities compared to traditional approaches, significantly reducing
technical complexities and accelerating the development of conversational systems.
Yet, there have been few systematic investigations into the components of
conversations and why certain models excel in this area, partly due to the
limitation of current research methods that are often reliant on pre-defined labels
in controlled datasets. This work seeks to address this limitation by developing a
role-defined framework for open-domain conversations that can be effectively
trained using role-defined datasets without pre- labels through an iterative
training process. The proposed framework, which is based on role-defined data,
can also automatically determine the relevance of utterances during the
training process, is then followed by an analysis of model performance using
supervised and self-improvement strategies. The results show that models
adversarially trained can achieve better performance on conversation coherence,
while models that engage in self-improvement perform significantly better in
conversation coherence and also excel in other metrics such as conversation
 richness and responsiveness.

The notion that stars exploding as supernovae leave behind compact objects, such as black holes and neutron stars, which produce gravitational waves when they merge, has led researchers to investigate the random background pattern of gravitational waves in the universe. Emerging theories suggest that the universe might contain a background pattern of gravitational waves, known as the "gravitational wave memory background," which was previously proposed to originate from ancient high-energy collisions involving black or neutron stars. A new study explores an alternative proposal that these collisions and subsequent mergers of compact objects, including those thought to occur during structure formation in the early universe, give rise to this background pattern. The research quantifies the amplitude of this background pattern within the frequency range of 10^-6 to 10^-4 Hz and observes that it could be detectable using future gravitational wave detectors like LISA.

If a hypothetical phase transition occurs within the universe's early history, it may create a distinct, peV-mass force carrier that causes high-energy leptons to be produced at exceptionally high rates. This could manifest as an unusual, diffuse gamma-ray signal in the Milky Way, and is predicted to be accompanied by ripples in the gravitational fabric of the universe, potentially detectable by future sensitive detectors. Additionally, the universe may harbor hidden, dense regions known as dark holes that could give rise to the observed peV-mass photons.

A fundamental inquiry in knowledge graph learning involves reconstructing causal relationships and semantic connections within complex scenarios. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach that integrates symbolic and symbolic causal inference methods to establish explicit, transparent causal links between high-level concepts. By merging these methods with an signaling game technique, we enable the discovery of hidden causal relationships between visible concepts, effectively transferring knowledge and enabling symbolic reasoning. Through applications on synthetic and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the ability of our framework to reveal implicit patterns and make predictions in practical scenarios.

The ability to predict document volume (term forecasting), particularly in an ad-hoc and top-down classification context, plays a critical role in developing Pre-ranking algorithms. Researchers have proposed a combination of Machine Learning techniques and Information Retrieval approaches to tackle this challenge, but a unified framework is still absent. To address this gap, we introduce a new approach that integrates a Non-parametric Naive Bayes classifier with Latent topics and Mixed Membership models, aiming to leverage their respective strengths. Our results demonstrate that a three-stage hybrid model, comprising Document-Level Training, Index-Level Training, and Live testing, is essential to achieving high accuracy. Experimenting with real-world data from Yahoo and The New York Times news articles, we achieve a remarkable 94% Mean Absolute Error (MAE) at a low computational cost, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods by over 10%.

Recent advancements in session-based recommendation research have highlighted the importance of sequential patterns in session data. As a result, state-of-the-art models are now beginning to incorporate rank-based representations of candidate items, offering improved performance and more meaningful insights. However, the development of enhanced rank-based candidate rank representations for session-based recommendation remains a neglected area of study. In response, we introduce a novel two-phase approach that utilizes rank-based representations to enhance the candidate items in each session. Our proposed method consists of an initial rank-based sampling phase and a subsequent ranking phase, where a established session-based model is re-trained to perfection on the sampled data. Through extensive experimentation on diverse datasets, we demonstrate that our approach significantly boosts state-of-the-art performance across multiple evaluation metrics.

In recent years, researchers have become increasingly interested in the internal dynamics of soft and hard colloidal particles, particularly in the presence of varying chemical activity levels. This interest stems from the fact that common fluids often exhibit varying levels of chemical activity, whether it's due to concentration differences or other factors, like heat. In our study, we've explored how the internal dynamics of colloidal systems are affected by a gradual decrease or increase in chemical activity, using a combination of theoretical and numerical approaches. Our results reveal the existence of an optimal activity level for a given colloidal particle that minimizes its internal movement. If the activity level exceeds this optimal point, the particle's internal movement actually increases. Additionally, our findings show that the response of the particle's internal dynamics to changes in activity is influenced by its size and the strength of interactions between neighboring particles. On the other hand, when activity levels decrease, the particle's internal movement is less responsive to changes in temperature. This research sheds new light on the behavior of soft and hard colloidal systems and provides a foundation for understanding the internal dynamics of particles in a wide range of chemical environments.

A thorough approach is described for computationally modeling the flow of single-phase fluids through three-dimensional fractured rock. The proposed methodology employs a novel time-stepping strategy, combining finite volume and finite difference techniques, to solve the conservative divergence equation on a multi-dimensional network of connected nodes. To achieve high accuracy in the solution, the conservativity of the numerical divergence operator is rigorously validated. To handle complex fractures, a flexible modeling approach is taken, where the fractures are treated as distinct spatial domains defined by surface representations. The interfaces between these fracture domains are treated as part of the global nonlinear problem via a conventional "ink pen" method, ensuring no fracture flooding occurs without physical penetration. A Conforming Multi-Dimensional Multi- dimensional Network is used to establish a seamless connection between the various fracture domains. To establish a convergent numerical approach, a consistent and penultimate time-stepping method is employed, paired with a stable and penultimate time-stepping method for solving the discrete problem on each fracture. Several numerical experiments are conducted to verify the approach, using both a 2D and 3D scenarios, involving various fracture configurations. The models are validated by comparing the numerical solutions with the respective analytical solutions, as well as through a comparison with existing public models in both 2D and 3D. The results show that the approach can achieve high accuracy in the solution with minimal error, using a reasonably sized network of nodes.

This study introduces an innovative technique for aligning a swarm of autonomous drones with a dynamic, moving shape within a 2D environment. The approach prioritizes maintaining the structural integrity of the aligned cluster throughout the alignment process. Additionally, a featureless representation method based on centroid point sets enables seamless relocation of the aligned cluster without generating "fences" that could obstruct the convergence of drones. Furthermore, a simplified yet effective collision avoidance system is integrated into the alignment process, leveraging local information and a heuristic strategy at each drone's local coordinate system to navigate around obstacles and maintain a safe distance from other drones. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments using a simulation tool and a swarm of drones composed of Racing F1 robots and Ring Cameras.

For a walk-based node-weighting scheme, the Seidel energy of a graph is defined as the sum of the absolute values of the seismic coefficients related to a walk-based kernel. We investigate the Seidel energy of a graph, where the kernel is derived from a set of normal walk sequences. The range of Seidel energies for a given number of sequences is determined and it's shown that this upper limit can be near linear to the number of vertices. Additionally, the Seidel energy of a graph created by combining two disjoint unions of regular bipartite graphs is characterized. The result includes a formula for the Seidel energy of the join of two graphs, where the Seidel energy of the join of two graphs with equal size and degree umbrality is determined as the quadruple of the original graphs' energies. For the join of two graphs with different sizes, the Seidel energy is expressed as a linear combination of the energies of the larger and smaller graphs.

This research presents a novel mean-field game consisting of a mean-field control problem for stochastic differential equations with delays, driven by fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter greater than 0.5. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control, along with the corresponding Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, under the assumptions of Lipschitz and high-order continuity. A compactness method is employed to prove the convergence of a specific discretized problem from our work in "Systems & Control Letters".

For the Dirac operator on a complete Riemannian manifold with a potentially negative vector field, we develop a new approach to understanding the finite-band operator and its relation to a linked self-adjoint operator. This connection allows us to study the finite-band operator as a limit of a connected family of embedded Dirac operators. Our findings include a proof of the connectedness of band edges and the existence of band edges as limits of connected families of embedded Dirac operators. These results also generalize to higher-band operators, where we find that the largest band edges form a connected set.

This research paper will present an in-depth analysis of a two-tier vehicle network architecture that utilizes integrated road-side components and vehicle relays. The primary goal of this system is to provide reliable connectivity to vehicles within urban areas, meeting the growing communications needs of these vehicles. The architecture's design philosophy is rooted in diversity, using road-side components and vehicle relays to enhance the network's capacity, reduce congestion, and ensure seamless data transmission. This architecture's functionality will be examined in relation to IoT applications that vehicles may utilize. The analysis will also focus on chiming patterns, relative delays, and pricing schemes as potential tools to mitigate malicious activities and unhealthy behaviors within the network. The findings of this study will provide insights into the practical applications of this architecture and offer potential solutions to related issues.

Wikipedia's vast knowledge, comprised of 50 million articles and 230 million paragraphs, is freely accessible but poses a major challenge due to the time-consuming process of searching for high-quality information. This study aims to mitigate this issue by developing a machine-readable guide that points to Wikipedia's high-quality content, tagged by editable sections such as summaries, references, and images. To achieve this, the research analyzes editing behaviors and their impact on articles, identifying patterns that predict and differentiate between high-quality and low-quality content. Based on these findings, a machine-learning model is trained to predict and characterize sections of poor quality, providing Wikipedia editors with insights to inform their revisions and maintaining the platform's integrity.

Artificial intelligence systems in safety-sensitive domains like aviation require robust assurance that their actions are predictable and aligned with human values. A decision-based black-box approach presents an alternative framework for building such systems, focusing on the results of their actions rather than the underlying reasoning processes. In this paper, we establish that this black-box approach is effective in creating reliable systems by demonstrating its similarity to rule-based systems, as well as by considering the computational challenges involved in validating its decisions. Additionally, we highlight the current limitations of the black-box framework, particularly in scenarios where additional assumptions are not applicable, and explore the feasibility of adapting a knowledge base from another domain to facilitate knowledge transfer in a decision-based black-box setting. An open-source implementation of our techniques, known as DB3, is also available online.

The decay processes of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K_S^0$, $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K_S^0$, $B^0_s\to D^0 \bar{K}^0$, and $B^0_s\to D^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ are investigated through the analysis of 37.4 fb^-1 data, collected from the LHCb experiment with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The observed branching fractions for $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K_S^0$ and $B^0_s\to D^0 \bar{K}^0$ are determined and compared with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the calculated ratio of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K_S^0$ to $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K_S^0$ is found to be in agreement with previous studies.

We apply the method of geometric t-duality to analyze t-duals of internal spacetimes within lower-dimensional string theories featuring twisted tori, circle bundles, and nilmanifolds as key components. Our analysis reveals that t-duals of these manifolds are distinct in nature, encompassing nilmanifolds, twisted tori, and circle bundles over nilmanifolds. To further establish its utility, we provide explicit examples in nilpotent orbifolds, showcasing t-duals of the type $\mathbb{R}^{1,1}$ $\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^{2}$, and $\mathbb{R}V_{8}$, whose t-duals can be identified as $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ $\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^{2}$, and $\mathbb{R}^{1,1}$, respectively.

Recent advances in peer teaching between robots have proven promising, but the existing research has been limited to scenarios where robots receive extensive training from their peers. To take this concept further, our proposed method aims to facilitate learning between robots without requiring a seasoned mentor to provide demonstrations. Instead, we allow the student robot to benefit from its experienced partner's accomplishments, and through repeated observations, the student robot is able to grasp essential task strategies. By leveraging the advantages offered by multiple observers, including the experienced mentor, the student robot is able to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the task at hand. Our results reveal that the student robot is able to achieve notable improvement with just a single observation from its mentor, and when paired with additional observations from its fellow robots, the student robot is able to achieve remarkable performance.

This paper explores the computational complexities of coding techniques to create secure systems that resist aggressive side-channel attacks. Specifically, we investigated the asymptotic performance of Provable Accountability Code (PAC) under two distinct metrics for evaluating attack resistance and code efficiency. Notably, PAC codes were shown to be resilient against a powerful form of side-channel attack known as Leaky Computation, offering an alternative perspective on this issue.

In this work, we develop a novel approach for real-time monitoring and updating hand-object interactions from a series of depth point cloud data, similar to those captured by devices such as Microsoft Kinect in a outdoor environment. Our method is designed to be efficient, processing around 33 frames per millisecond. It consists of three key components: a hand model, a tracking algorithm, and a reconstruction technique. The hand model is built using a simplified template and adjusted to fit the actual hand shape, using a combination of geometric and kinematic information. This adjusted hand shape is then used to determine the hand's pose in 3D space. A tracking algorithm based on a general-invariant representation of the hand's shape is used to calculate the hand's movement and pose across consecutive frames. Any discrepancies between the hand's pose and actual movement are detected and the hand's pose is adjusted accordingly. The reconstructed hand pose is then used to track and update hand-object interactions. Our method is particularly versatile and can be applied to various tasks, such as counting and classifying hand-object interactions. Our study includes a comprehensive evaluation of the accuracy of our approach for tracking and reconstructing hand object engagements, using a dataset of 40 complex interactions between multiple hands and objects. Our method is compared to a more traditional approach, based on an image-based representation, and found to be more accurate and efficient.

A type of geometric configuration known as a C-collection, a concept that has its roots in Coxeter groups, consists of specific arrangements of elements in a Euclidean space. Those that can be formed through a series of reflections, where the reflections involved correspond to the elements in a corresponding diagram, are referred to as attainable; those that can be reached in this manner are referred to as noncrystallographic. We are studying here a specific set of attainable C_collections, specifically those with a rank of 4 and an interleaving number of 2, based on a certain triangle configuration. We determine the specific sets of elements, or roots, that can be used for the reflections in this case. We also establish that the maximal symmetry in these configurations corresponds to one of five possible types: A4, M4, SL2(C3), M3:2, or M22. We further classify the C_collections, or configurations, based on their symmetry groups.

A robot's ability to perform tasks efficiently near objects is often hindered by calibration difficulties. Many modern robots rely on depth sensors to simplify the calibration process, allowing them to accurately calculate object positions and pose without additional equipment. Nevertheless, the accuracy of depth measurements is usually insufficient for precise task execution, prompting the development of advanced algorithms that can compensate for depth sensor errors. This paper introduces an innovative method that leverages machine learning to estimate end-effector positions from raw depth data, eliminating the need for time-consuming and expensive calibration procedures. By converting the pose estimation task into a continuous problem and applying a neural network, the proposed algorithm can quickly and accurately calculate end-effector positions. Furthermore, the method enables robots to adjust their viewing positions to minimize measurement errors based on predicted object poses. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in estimating end-effector positions with subcentimeter accuracy.

A new framework, K-Nearest-Neighbors (KNN) Interference, has been introduced to model the effects of treatment disruption by analyzing the impact on a target individual. This framework considers the interference it uses as a stylized model of treatment disruption, where the interference's area of influence and its adjustment for spatial proximity are key components. Under this framework, the conceptual identification framework provides general conditions under which treatment disruption can be identified from available data. These conditions are divided into two main groups: one that requires a specific model be estimable and another that imposes conditions directly on the data. Several statistical methods have been proposed to identify treatment disruption in practice. A key finding from our investigation is that unlike the model-dependent method, the data-driven methods we proposed do not rely on accurate modeling but rather rely on data that is often readily available. This is particularly notable because one of our methods relies solely on nonparametric information, making it applicable in a wider range of contexts.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from dark matter interactions within neutron stars are revised, focusing on cases mediated by light pseudoscalar messengers. While previous studies assumed dark matter primarily resided within the star's core, our findings reveal that the entire neutron star is affected by dark matter interactions. As a result, predicted neutrino emissions from dark matter annihilations within neutron stars are increased by up to 17 orders of magnitude, depending on the model's parameters. These improvements lead to significantly higher limits on the dark matter-nucleon interaction strength, applied differentially to the dark matter's various spin states. Consequently, these restrictions now fall within the same range as direct detection limits. Additionally, improved modeling of neutrino emissions from dark matter interactions within neutron stars is expected to refine estimates of the neutron star cooling time. Therefore, these revised neutrino emissions could potentially be used to test the hypothesis that dark matter is composed of WIMP-like particles.

The ongoing UNIONS survey, combining data from the CFIS and Legacy SF0 projects, has made extensive observations of 6729.9 square degrees in the Northern sky, collecting 69.1 million galaxies with high accuracy in photometry and shape measurement. This extensive dataset is essential for conducting systematic shape information necessary for cosmological analyses based on galaxy surveys. To ensure reliable results, a thorough-shape-assessment pipeline is required to eliminate biases and increase precision. The paper introduces a new, robust pipeline, ShapePipe, that utilizes multiple techniques such as galaxy morphology classification, galaxy size adjustment, and shape measurement validation to ensure reliable results. Additionally, the pipeline successfully applies shape information to conduct a weak-lensing analysis of the galaxy catalog, allowing for the creation of a highly accurate map of the galaxy bias and the cosmic microwave background lensing convergence, all achieved without integrating any external data.

One of the most influential number theory findings within the 20th century was the resolution of the Hannah problem, which dated back to the 19th century. The main aim of this paper was to expand on the work begun by Li and Zheng in 2018, regarding an extension of the Hannah problem. Li and Zheng had considered an infinite sum related to complex roots of non-normal polynomials. This paper seeks to resolve a more complex challenge, by examining an even more extensive infinite sum that involves complex roots of non-normal polynomials. The results of the work carried out here enable a precise estimate of the magnitude of the error term. A crucial aspect of the study was the application of a novel equidistribution finding, concerning one-dimensional tori. This new finding represents an expansion of the work begun by Li and Zheng. The proof of the results obtained here, involves a combination of the work carried out by Li and Zheng, along with key concepts drawn from the works of Iwaniec, Jones, Brüdern, and Chow.
We prove that for k-rational singularities, k-Du Bois singularities, and k-Epsilon Del Pezzo fibrations, k can be replaced by any greater k'.

Research into systems that exhibit Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transitions has primarily focused on materials whose spin-inertia is fixed and non-interacting components. Contrary to this trend, our study presents an analysis of a flexible Heisenberg spin system that transitions from a non-biquadratic interaction to a quadratic one, in the presence of an external magnetic field. Surprisingly, the system reveals both static and dynamic signs of BKT-related behavior, even when the spin-inertia remains quadratic. This finding confirms that the BKT phase transition is not unique to systems with non-fixed spin-inertia and that it can also occur in higher-spin systems, potentially expanding the range of materials in which it can occur.

In certain cosmic environments, ultralight bosons may develop nearly 0-point fluctuations that act as a form of'shadow matter', affecting the gravitational interaction between regular matter and dark matter. A specific example involves the axion-like particle, a key component of the axion dark matter theory. This paper examines the impact of such a particle on the structure and evolution of the Universe, using simulations to model a cosmic void. It finds that if the particle is present, a region with its current mass density would experience an increase in pressure, leading to altered matter distribution. A corresponding increase in matter density within a composite object such as a galaxy would result in an enhanced gravitational force, directing matter towards the center. This process would result in a compact, star-like object forming at the center of the void. A detectable signal would be produced in the form of a radio beacon by any object forming in this way. A possible candidate for this phenomenon is a star-like object observed in the direction of the NGC 4261 galaxy, which could be explained by the interaction of regular matter and dark matter, including a 1 microeV particle. This particle would also cause a detectable anomaly in the light passing through the galaxy, due to its being a relativistic cosmological object. A particle of this mass would also leave behind imprints in the form of observable rotations of galaxy clusters and a faint redshifted radio signal, which could serve as a confirmation of the predicted model. A possible indication

We assess the performance of certain classes of quantum error correction codes, specifically those based on the magic states of cluster-connected qubits. Our study focuses on the distillable entanglement that can be achieved through the use of stabilizer operations, particularly those supported by the magic states. Under the assumption that the states in question are grouptypical with respect to the symmetric group, we're able to establish more stringent bounds on the distillable entanglement. Our findings supplement previous research by Robert and Breuer, who had previously established limits under the assumption that the states in question are random and uniformly distributed within their respective groups.

Utilizing the Tsallis distribution, we investigate how thermal quantum fields transform into holographic black holes in Randall-Sundrum models under a new form of quintessence method. The approach involves introducing a complex scalar field, where its real component acts as a quintessence field and, when imaginary, generates a gauge field. The method employs thermodynamic properties of the black hole to determine the temperature and other constants of the Tsallis distribution. The results in the Euclidean black hole scenario reveal that as the temperature decreases, the Tsallis parameter expands and shifts towards the Einstein gravity. The AdS black hole scenario exhibits a similar trend but with an additional effect, where the parameter expands due to the impact of the quintessence field's strength. Conversely, in the Melvin universe scenario, the Tsallis parameter contracts when the temperature decreases, indicating a shift from the Tsallis gravity towards the Einstein gravity. The analysis in all scenarios demonstrates that as the parameter shifts towards the Einstein gravity, the thermal radiation transitions into holographic dark energy.

The Large Sky Survey to study the astrophysical objects on a large scale has also begun to explore the time domain, leveraging the LAMOST Telescope's multi-object spectrographic capabilities. To do this, the project has incorporated a new approach, employing a moving object's changing spectral features to determine its velocity and potential variability. To initiate this effort, the project observed four areas, capturing four epochs of data, which led to the identification and analysis of 1,500 objects changing in a certain property. These objects' characteristics fall within a specific range, and their motion is being tracked in a data set that is available online. Among these objects, 94% map to a specific type of star, and their movement is being tracked in a data set that is available online. These initial findings suggest that the approach effectively identifies both moving stars that change in a certain way and external factors affecting a star, which are then recorded in a data set that is available online.

Unpredictable noise from various sources within a system typically has negative consequences on its randomness. This study introduces TuRaN, a novel randomized bit generation approach, which utilizes undervoltage in static RAM to produce high-quality random bits. The primary goal of TuRaN is to mitigate the detrimental effect of manufacturing defects on random bit generation. The technique takes advantage of existing undervoltage in energy-efficient CMOS technology to generate random bits, thereby eliminating the need for additional power consumption. The reliability of random bit generation is ensured by means of an external quality assessment circuit connected directly to the main processing unit via a data bus. Additionally, various testing methods have been developed to verify the randomness of the generated bits, incorporating both traditional statistical analysis and machine learning-based techniques. The results show that TuRaN can operate at under 25% of the standard voltage while still producing high-quality random bits, meeting the standards set by the Advanced Encryption Standard algorithm. The current implementation has a maximum frequency of 1.33 MHz and was tested using a 65nm CMOS technology. The research was conducted without considering energy consumption, a factor that could potentially impact the efficiency of the approach.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron non-volatile relay has been developed, incorporating two molecular monolayers with distinct conductance levels. The first, made of methanol, serves as a quasi-one-dimensional wire, while the second, composed of para-hydroquinone-based molecules, functions as a non-volatile switch. The relay's architecture, comprised of a metal/solid interface, allows it to be programmed and used in computational circuits that operate through the movement of single electrons. The reliability of the design has been assessed through multiple simulations that considered various monolayer properties and the presence of traps at the metal/solid interface. The results show that the molecular single-electron relay can be efficiently used in circuits that require minimal power consumption and are resistant to radiation, operating at extremely low temperatures and with high storage capacities.

We develop a novel, imaginative representation of complex Feynman integrals, 
which serves as the underlying basis for all numerical evaluation methods 
and is particularly useful for identifying the underlying parameters that 
need to be evaluated numerically. This imaginative representation is then 
applied to multi-loop Feynman integrals, which are broken down into simpler 
components based on loop momenta connections. The complexity of Feynman 
integrals is analyzed and ranked by the number of underlying parameters, 
with an innovative approach for parameter reduction through integration 
processes. This framework is then used for a thorough numerical evaluation 
of the planar double-box integral. The implementation details and the 
resulting code are also provided.

We derive an expression to extrapolate basis eigenfunctions of the one-dimensional Dirac equation across multiple discrete momentum values, which are commonly found in quantum stride models. This formula can be applied to both non-relativistic and Galerkin approximations of the eigenfunctions. We verify its accuracy by comparing it with numerical solutions obtained using a finite element method and analyze its computational convergence.

In a theoretical framework, nuclear and quark matter equilibria are modeled using the $s$-$\omega$-$\rho$ gauge principle, combined with the Polyakov-Landau-Kalisky model. This approach yields a hybrid kernel from the combination of the MIT bag model and the NJL model. By incorporating a heat bath of quarks and diquarks, the model successfully replicates the phase diagram of  np$^-$ quark matter, with a first-order transition line and associated soft mode instability for symmetric nuclear matter. Additionally, the model considers the influence of gauge boson mass and decay mode on the equation of state and phase diagram.

This paper examines a $q$-deformed optomechanical system where the movement of a mirror is influenced by heated photons. We investigate how the value of $q$ affects the transfer of light and energy within the system. We also explore the impact of $q$ on the cooling of a mechanical oscillator in two optomechanical configurations, focusing on the distinction between high-frequency and low-frequency oscillations. We ultimately reveal how the value of $q$ can lead to improved transmission and cooling in optomechanical systems by modifying their physical properties.

In a model where nuclear and supersymmetric particles have similar properties, there's a type of adverse R-parity phenomenon observed within a type of nuclear deformation, known as the Double-Rotors Model. During this occurrence, an R-parity-conserving process appears to violate R-parity due to the differing R-parity values of the initial and final states, which is then exacerbated by the presence of a nonsymmetric nuclear force interaction. Utilizing a weak-coupling limit approach, researchers estimated the scarcity of R-parity violation signatures in scissors modes, which is then compared to experimental findings, revealing that these violations align with observed data. To confirm the Double-Rotors Model, future experiments could focus on searching for R-parity violation signatures in scissors modes, which could also have implications for supersymmetric particle searches.

The chemistry of transition metal oxides is highly complex and influential due to various energy state variations that are still not fully understood. Investigations have shown that the properties of these states vary significantly in a single crystal layer, suggesting that ultra-thin transition metal oxides have immense potential for applications in nanotechnology. We have observed multiple energy state variations in ultra-thin MgO and FeO layers and found that their surface structures greatly affect the occurrences and patterns of these variations. Furthermore, we have found that the variations in these states are closely linked to the variations in magnetic properties, which makes them suitable for use in magnetic memory technologies.

A new type of discrete differential transformation, inspired by the fractional ordinary differential equation, is developed and applied to a driven optical lattice where coolated atoms are subjected to non-local dissipation. This drive can be seen as a special case of the fractional derivative, where the order is not present. The fractional derivative is typically associated with long-range interactions, where potential falls off rapidly, often inversely with the second power of the distance. This model is then used to investigate the anomalous diffusion of atoms in this setup, where initial findings indicate non-ergodic behavior characterized by a constant, non-zero long-time diffusion coefficient despite the absence of normal diffusion. Furthermore, the observed statistics show temperature dependence that varies directly with the square of the driving power, a phenomenon not observed in other non-dissipative optical lattices. This study provides a foundation for further exploration into the application of the discrete fractional derivative in modeling physical systems and its potential ties to long-range interactions.

This study investigates the hierarchy within a cryptocurrency exchange network by analyzing relationships between various cryptocurrencies. The research begins with an extensive trading network that encompasses all cryptocurrencies traded on major exchanges. Each unique cryptocurrency is labeled as a node in the network, with edges representing transaction links between nodes. By examining the exchange habits of all pairs of cryptocurrencies, the research identifies direct relationships between the nodes. The analysis reveals that many cryptocurrencies are linked directly with fewer than 13 other nodes, while a smaller number of popular cryptocurrencies have numerous trading connections. The research also demonstrates that higher-order relationships among groups of cryptocurrencies exist, with some (such as Bitcoin and Ethereum) being central to their respective communities. The study further finds that when including indirect relationships, the popularity of certain cryptocurrencies increases, while their relative positions within their respective communities do not change. The implications of these findings are then considered in the context of a theoretical model that captures the complex interplay between popular and less-traded cryptocurrencies. The study concludes by reflecting on the societal aspects of this cryptocurrency exchange landscape.

The formation of small sulfuric acid and water clusters plays a significant role in atmospheric chemistry. To gain insight into their structure, the interaction between dipolar molecules was investigated through the application of symmetry-preserving perturbation theory at the level of Hartree-Fock. This study analyzed the influence of temperature and pressure on these clusters, also comparing the roles of harmonic and anharmonic motion using the simulated values of Raman spectra. The results showed that even at relatively high concentrations of water, sulfuric acid dominates the composition of the smallest clusters. This study's findings contradict earlier experiments that suggested a preference for neutral clusters composed of equal parts water and sulfuric acid. The calculations attributed this discrepancy to the significant vibrational motion of sulfuric acid dimerions, which broadens the associated rotational energy levels and affects their energy more significantly than harmonic motion, especially for the smallest clusters. This study's results suggest that anharmonic motion is responsible for the experimental observations of sulfuric acid dimerions.

We introduce an operator $\widehat{\mathscr{C}}$ that compacts operator pairs $(T_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}$ with $T_\alpha$ being group equivariant non-dilating operators on $L^2(\Sigma_\mu)$. Given a countable group $\Gamma$, let $\mu$ be a finite measure on $\Sigma_\mu=\widehat{\Gamma}$, the dual of $\Gamma$. The operator $\widehat{\mathscr{C}}$ maps the isometry orbit $\mathscr{I}T$ of an operator $T$ to the operator space $\mathscr{R}T_\mu$. Here, the operator space $\mathscr{R}T_\mu$ consists of all $\Gamma$-equivariant non-dilating operators on $L^2(\Sigma_\mu)$ that have the same amplification as $T_\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in A$. The main part of the research shows that $\widehat{\mathscr{C}}$ satisfies two key properties. Firstly, it transforms isometry orbits of compactness. Secondly, it transforms amenability orbits of operator spaces $\mathscr{R}T_\mu$. To prove these claims, we need to prove that the stationary non-dilating operator technique works for certain operator spaces $\mathscr{R}T_\mu$. This involves developing a novel stationary non-dilating operator method.

In classical physics, Newtonian gravity mirrors the dynamics of a point charge, which is consistent with the behavior seen in quantum mechanics when observing the canonical anticommutation relations of operators within a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. However, this similarity fails in the quantum regime, especially when considering the canonical anticommutation relations of operators within an infinite-dimensional state space, as demonstrated by the thermal Hall effect. This phenomenon arises through a combination of geometric curvature and non-inertial motion, which is equivalent to a Robertson-Walker metric with a de Sitter universe. Despite this, the relationship between canonical fl fl and canonical fl components does not adhere to Einstein's gravitational analogy. Furthermore, the energy density and pressure do not satisfy the conditions required for gravitational analogy.

Our theory posits that complex neural networks' performance is largely due to various complex geometric constraints, which include multiple regularity parameters, unlike the commonly referred to weight decay. This study introduces multiple new regularization parameters, such as continuity, smoothness, and shape parameters, that improve model interpretability and promote generalization. We illustrate the significance of each parameter through well-designed experiments and demonstrate that increasing the number of geometric constraints leads to better generalization. Additionally, we propose a comprehensive search space for all these regularization parameters, which results in highly efficient performance. Notably, our findings also suggest that overparameterization is not the primary factor contributing to successful neural networks, as geometric intricacy plays a more crucial role.

In the context of automated composition evaluation, data augmentation, a technique used to boost training a model's performance by generating artificial data from available labels, is explored in this research. A novel data augmentation approach is developed for a specific type of automated composition evaluation, which typically relies on short, discrete input data. The newly proposed method employs a BERT-based transformer model to artificially diversify the generated musical data. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through multiple experiments using various data augmentation techniques and benchmarking a subsequent training with augmented data. The findings suggest that the application of this data augmentation strategy yields a significant improvement in the evaluated model's performance.

The use of copula models has become the standard approach for modeling multivariate distributions and studying joint probability calculations. The models are highly flexible, allowing for the creation of tailored distributions through marginal probability models. The first step in this approach involves selecting a copula, followed by a corresponding set of marginal probability models. The newly formed multivariate probability model is then used to describe the joint behavior of the variables. This research paper focuses on a broad framework for analyzing univariate probability models and their associated dependencies, which serves as the initial step in the copula framework. The marginal dependence frameworks presented here consist of various methods to measure the dependence between two variables, each method providing a different perspective on their interaction. The results obtained can lead to the development of a practical method for choosing the most suitable copula model from a given set of candidates, based on the observed properties of the data. The work presented here is further applied to simulate independent data from specified univariate distributions, which serves as a starting point for future research on dependent data.

This research explores a dynamic model of social mobility where multiple generations of agents strive to achieve their desired life standards, with each generation making decisions based on the previous one's achievements. A prospect theory-based utility function, sensitive to gains and losses, is used to model the decisions of these multi-agent dynamics. To gain insights into the potential outcomes of this model, we investigate a self-consistent approach and develop a framework for analyzing the model's equilibrium points. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate how the model's solutions are affected by various parameters, such as initial conditions and the level of risk aversion. Notably, our results show that in a setting with only two levels of risk tolerance, the distribution of achievements exhibits oscillatory behavior over time, characterized by periods of increasing and decreasing trends.

The relationship between parity and statistics, acting on a non-relativistic one-dimensional wavefunction, directly determines the spin statistics theorem when applied to a particle of mass $m$ with momentum $p$ and energy $E$, where $E = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, based on the properties of the commutator $[p, E] = 0$.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity as other, non-consensus based methods, due to its inability to hide transaction amounts, it still offers a level of anonymity for regular users, due to its consensus-based design, for which we provide a detailed analysis.

The rapidly growing field of deep learning has reached new heights in processing complex data, however, its application to numerous fields of study remains under exploration. Researchers are particularly interested in using deep learning to tackle longstanding challenges in computer science, such as developing new algorithms for linear equation solving. While many algorithms are highly efficient, they often fail to perform well in the rare case of extremely large matrix sizes. To address this issue, a novel approach, called Structured Vector-Valued Neural Networks, is proposed to improve solving linear equations with unique properties. By incorporating expert knowledge, this network enhances performance on both theoretical and practical problems involving sparse, permutation, and skew-symmetric matrices. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating problem-specific structures into neural networks can significantly revitalize the efficiency of solving linear equations, especially for large spaces.

A highly anticipated electromagnetic interaction, describing the simultaneous exchange of three gauge bosons, is theoretically confirmed for its first-ever observation. Utilizing the LHCb detector, a comprehensive analysis of 1.45 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV was conducted to provide a precise test of the predicted interaction mechanism. By categorizing events corresponding to the desired interaction, a statistical advantage was gained over background occurrences. The signal-to-noise ratio for the desired interaction mechanism was found to be 3.54 standard deviations above background. Further data collection is anticipated to yield a statistically significant observation of the interaction mechanism.

In 2014, the Hebrew Universal Dependencies treebank was introduced, representing a significant effort in translating the widely-used CoNLL/UD format to the Hebrew language. Over the past nine years, this treebank has undergone continuous improvement with updates, but have remained inactive since 2018. This lack of progress is being addressed by presenting new and revised annotations for both the original and new texts added since the last update. These updates total 366 new sentences, spanning 4613 tokens and 4190 dependencies. The enhanced treebank now comprises 2326 sentences, 28691 tokens, and 27394 dependencies. The new and revised annotations will significantly improve Hebrew's representation in the UD ecosystem, particularly through the integration of modern linguistic theories and the application of UD guidelines. Additionally, this updated treebank will facilitate research in areas such as UD-based tasks, enhancing Hebrew's exposure in international NLP competitions like SemEval and CoLA. The improved treebank will also promote the development of advanced NLP systems in Hebrew, covering tasks like parsing and machine translation.

We establish that for any $p$ within the range $1 < p < \infty$, a given subspace $\cal F$ of $\ell_p$, and a given $\varepsilon$ greater than zero, there exists an $\varepsilon$-isometric mapping $\Phi$ that preserves sparsity from $\cal F$ into $\ell_p$. The dimension of the image under $\Phi$ is at most a function of $\varepsilon$, and the funtion it maps to, is independent of $p$.

Recent advancements in numerical modeling have enabled the utilization of computational models in the collaborative scientific workflow.  This paper introduces a proposed framework that combines data-informed computational models to facilitate collaborative modeling.  This framework, based on a multi-physics approach, uses discrete element method and discrete element-continuum method models which are paired with experimental data from particle image velocimetry.  By effectively integrating both numerical and experimental results, the developed model can predict the behavior of masses suspended in a fluid flow driven by an oscillating plate.  This approach is exemplified through a case study of the prediction of a titanium alloy particle's motion.

Research into linear coding systems that utilize binary signals to transmit data over an unreliable communication channel, resulting in random error patterns, has led to the development of an innovative density multiplicity-based Low-density parity-check code. This code, constructed by merging the properties of a Low-density parity-check code and a degree-degree coded code, exhibits enhanced performance on the binary erasure channel, as evidenced by our numerical results. Furthermore, we verified that the code's versatility extends beyond the binary erasure channel, as it also displays improved resistance to random errors on the binary symmetric channel.

For autonomous systems to safely operate in unpredictable situations, 
their components must be able to make predictions about their likely behavior.
This process, known as prognostics, not only provides time frames for when 
components are likely to fail but also gives exact dates, which helps 
predictive maintenance to be more efficient. Currently used prognostic methods 
are primarily non-safe as they rely on data that was previously collected and 
are not capable of being used during actual system operation. An important step 
in improving this has been made in this paper where tighter bounds on the 
predictive errors of a method for linear systems are calculated and its 
efficacy is evaluated under real world conditions. Additionally, this paper 
presents an alternative approach for predicting when failures will occur in 
linear systems. This approach uses a safety verified filter that is constantly 
making predictions about when parts of the system are likely to fail. The 
predictive errors of this approach are compared with currently used methods 
under real world conditions from the areas of prognostics and system level synthesis.

A critical component in the development of post-quantum cryptography is the distribution of quantum keys through advanced techniques like phase-encoding for enhancing secret key generation rates, as demonstrated in the phase-encoding quantum key distribution (PEQKD) system. However, maintaining the integrity of PEQKD is challenging when faced with an opponent who has access to the internal workings of the system, as they can exploit vulnerabilities to bypass the system's security. Recently, studies have shown that randomly fluctuating phases in PEQKD can be vulnerable to a sophisticated form of attack known as the reverse engineering attack. This has led to the investigation of an even more complex scenario, where an opponent manipulates both the internal workings and the external environment of the PEQKD system through unknown quantum states, potentially affecting both transmission channels. Our research focuses on evaluating the vulnerability of a new distribution method based on decoy states generated through partial phase randomization, aiming to establish a more secure transmission system for PEQKD.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated the effectiveness of a technique called in-context learning, allowing for specific tasks to be performed through a single input of examples rather than through weight adjustments. Our work focuses on evaluating the impact of training dataset quality and diversity on the learning capabilities of in-context learning models. By adding noise to a well-established dataset, we were able to manipulate its properties and observe its effect on model performance. Our findings reveal that using high-quality data leads to enhanced in-context learning capabilities, while data with inconsistent rules however does not necessarily hinder this capability. Conversely, increasing the variety of training data results in improved out-of-distribution robustness. Our work provides systematic insights into how training data influences the behavior of in-context learning models, offering potential guidelines for utilizing such models in real-world applications.

Galaxy formations are heavily influenced by the formation of their intergalactic environments. In this research, we simulate the long-term development (approximately 300 million years) of a galaxy group using cosmological simulations, focusing on the cooling of gas and its impact on the group's structure. To understand the role of radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction in the development of galaxy groups, we ran multiple simulations with various physical processes. The results reveal that without radiative cooling, gas within the group's interior over-accumulates, causing it to over-pressurize and ultimately lead to the group's breakup. In contrast, when this process is active but paired with magnetic fields that suppress gas movement, the group breaks up slowly. Furthermore, when thermal conduction is active but limited by a low threshold, the group breaks up more slowly than compared to scenarios with no cooling or magnetic restrictions. To gain a deeper understanding, we also analyzed the group's breakup based on the Chandrasekhar condition for gravitational instability. The results indicate that gas instability depends on the group's density and mass, and the breakdown of group structures occurs under specific ranges of these parameters. The research shows that when a group's density is high, it breaks up due to over-pressurization, but when it is dense but has a high mass, it holds together. The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the role of gas physics in the development of galaxy groups and their breakdown, and may

Utilizing the property of transposition in two-dimensional topological field theories, we derive a relationship between a three-dimensional invariant of a knot in a non-trivial state and its two-dimensional counterpart, an invariant of a link in a trivial state. This calculation is carried out through the application of the BRS operator to a off-shell action in a three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory, based on the gauge group $SU(2)/\mathbb{Z}_2$, in order to investigate the origins of the relationship. Having determined the connection between these two theories, we subsequently generalize our results to include higher degree homology classes. Our findings reveal that the relationship between these invariants is expressed through the use of the $Q$-operator, an auxiliary tool used in the study. Additionally, we derive a formula for the three-dimensional invariant of a knot in a non-trivial state by examining the homology classes associated with the one-cocycles of the hook type. These results are described in the context of a beautiful and elegant theory, characterized by its reliance on simple, easy-to-visualize objects, in the spirit of Edward Witten's 1994 Princeton University lectures.

New bosonic scattering amplitudes for strings have been calculated in superstring theory using a specific level one five-boson amplitude. Researchers found that a previously proposed formula by Gross is applicable to a broader range of amplitudes than previously thought. The obtained results confirm that the amplitude formulas for various interactions, including those for four-point and five-point grassmannian scattering, are the same as those calculated using established string theory methods. Additionally, the amplitudes were shown to be consistent with recently discovered relationships in superstring theory. Specifically, the amplitudes were found to be connected in a way that allows them to be combined into a single, more complex amplitude that is capable of describing a wider range of interactions. The study also identifies a fundamental relationship, which may have far-reaching implications for the study of scattering processes in general.

To effectively manage their resources, future cellular networks require sophisticated self-healing capabilities, integrating resource orchestration with real-time network reconfiguration through intelligent decision-making processes. Our work addresses the technical aspects of implementing these decision-making processes within a self-healing 5G core network framework, including self-sustaining mechanisms for network resource management and fault tolerance in radio access, as well as presenting results from a proof-of-concept implementation and experimental trials.

The objective of this research is to enable speech synthesis without language-specific data through a new transcription approach that identifies basic acoustic units directly from speech signals. These units are then used to establish a phonetic-to-acoustic model without the need for transcription, a task that is typically impossible without extensive language-specific training data. The proposed method was evaluated on two datasets, zero-resource language data, and comparison speech from a high-quality synthesizer, with recognition and transcription performance measured using various metrics. The results demonstrate its effectiveness in producing translations and synthesizing speech from these translations, with a level of accuracy comparable to a top-tier synthesizer.

A novel method combines McCormick envelope relaxation and mixed-integer convex optimization to enable efficient data-driven motion planning within complex environments. By leveraging a hybrid approach of exact and relaxed solutions for tight bounding, this technique generates a series of interconnected linearly independent problems. Each problem in this multi-stage optimization framework echoes a classic convex obstacle avoidance control problem, originally proposed by Breur et al. in 2015. This multi-stage optimization framework achieves a balance between the computational expense of exact solutions and the degree of relaxation tightness, making it suitable for solving large-scale planning issues. The proposed method is data-driven, meaning it doesn't require collecting information until after the planning stage. Instead, it derives necessary parameters for tight bounding using sample data from the environment. To showcase its effectiveness, this method was applied to a simulated self-driving scenario with software tools called IPOPT and Gurobi, producing results that could be executed within a few seconds.

We examine the process of a quantum state transitioning from a given initial state to a target state via sequential applications of quantum channels drawn from a predetermined set. By leveraging a resource theory approach, we identify the minimum amount of these channels needed to achieve this transformation, under either deterministic or probabilistic protocols, considering only channels that remain within a specified subset. Our analysis reveals a critical distinction between probabilistic and deterministic protocols, as we prove that, in some situations, there are no deterministic protocols, but there are always probabilistic ones, involving a finite number of steps, requiring only a limited number of channel draws, to achieve the target state. Furthermore, our findings extend to the case where target states are part of a continuum, and we also investigate the scenario where available channels are drawn from a broader, yet still restricted, set. By generalizing our approach, we apply these concepts to the case of multiple initial states, leading to the discovery of a region in a resource theory context, where the probabilistic convergence of these states falls within.

The behavior of coffee being spilled while carried in a cup has been analyzed through its vibration as a driven pendulum. The dynamics of the spilled coffee are observed to undergo a transition from a stable to an unstable state as the cup is moved under constant gravity, affecting the angle at which the coffee begins to spill. The Spill Angle Theory was developed to explain this phenomenon in conjunction with the Pendulum Theory. The theoretical models were validated through experimental observations of coffee and a professionally made mechanical replica of a cup, both mounted on a driving system. The theories predict the Spill Angle to be influenced by the ratio of the radius to the length and the type of driving motion, which was both measured and visualized through 2D and 3D simulations. The theories were further tested with additional experiments, including changing the spill direction, using an inertial fluid and altering the spill location on the cup's curvature.

In our research paper, we tackle the challenge of a specific decentralized learning issue by proposing a graph-based solution through the DR-DSGD method. Although Graph DSGD is a widely efficient approach for minimizing aggregate functions over networks via local gradient averaging, it assumes uniform data distribution within each node, which may not hold in real-world scenarios. Our graph DSGD protocol, DR-DSGD, addresses this limitation by leveraging the conceptual framework of representation learning to gauge distribution shifts. We note that mere statistics of representative nodes may not suffice to assess the graph-wide distributional change, so DR-DSGD proactively collects and locally averages the gradients from representative nodes at the beginning of each epoch to account for any data distribution variability. We derive a non-asymptotic rate of convergence for DR-DSGD based on specific criteria. Furthermore, our research is grounded in real-world data, which demonstrates the efficacy of DR-DSGD.

We introduce the concept of initial condition energy, revealing a fundamental connection between entropy production and gradient flow. This relation is utilized to devise a universal method for determining the amount of energy generated during relativistic nuclear collisions. By integrating the flow of entropy, we find that pullers create more final state energy than pushers. Using relativistic viscous fluid dynamics, we simulate two specific central collisions to quantify the generated energy, finding that pullers produce up to 4 times more energy than pushers.

We conducted a detailed analysis of the connection between high-speed jets and low-speed outflows using the MHD module in the ADAST code to simulate the early protostar phase. For the high-density case, high-speed jets helped to clear their surrounding material and maintained a fast velocity of ~100-1000 km/s even after interacting with the ambient medium, which is consistent with observational evidence. Furthermore, in the high-density scenario, high-speed jets successfully propelled low-speed outflows when the protostar's magnetic field reached a critical threshold, which is a significant phenomenon observed in real stars. High-speed jets can effectively drive low-speed outflows if the protostar's magnetic field is strong enough to withstand any slowing effect, which is a crucial finding for star formation research.

A dual approach known as "two-times' representation can describe the transient and stationary behaviors of a therapy intervention aimed at restoring equilibrium to a restricted nonlinear system, such as an electrical circuit with a shorted membrane, by analyzing its switch-regulated dynamics in a reduced phase-space. This dual approach consists of a transient, efficient regime and a stationary, over-saturated regime. It is proven that in the efficient regime, the system operates according to an expanded version of its original dynamics, while in the over-saturated regime, the system's dynamics are determined by a lower-dimensional version of its original dynamics. Additionally, it is possible to maintain a balance between these two regimes by adjusting the system parameters, thereby preventing the system from entering the over-saturated regime at the cost of reduced efficiency in the transient regime.

The Solar Radiation Pressure effect is gaining attention as a means to induce and exploit orbital elements evolution in artificial objects, which has significant implications for Space Debris Management and related topics. To account for the Solar Radiation Pressure's influence, researchers have developed various models, some leading to simple analytical results that capture the essence of the Solar radiation Pressure's impact under specific conditions. One such condition is the occurrence of the SRP-induced resonance, which can cause rapid and uncontrollable changes in an object's orbital elements, posing a threat to operational spacecraft and creating challenges for Space Debris Management. To gain a deeper understanding of the SRP's impact, researchers have also developed various numerical and analytical methods to model its effects accurately. One such approach, which combines high-order perturbation theory with numerical integration, has led to the development of several methods to quantify the SRP-induced effects, including the evaluation of the Solar radiation Pressure semi-secular resonances.

We examine the validity of a crucial assumption underpinning first-principles tight-binding models used to simulate electronic properties of systems undergoing rapid motion.  Under the condition that a system remains the same when subjected to spacetime symmetry transformations, our theoretical framework derives strict limits on the form of any electron-light interaction representation.  From this, we identify the specific restrictions which ensure the preservation of electron-light interaction models when applied to moving systems, thereby maintaining their physical integrity.  We subsequently test the relevance of our theoretical framework by simulating the motion of a charged particle in models based on 21-nanometer silicon structures, which were generated using a first-principles approach.  Furthermore, we extend our analysis by investigating non-relativistic electron-light interaction models in situations where both the electron and the photon do not follow traditional particle trajectories.  Our findings indicate that many from the vast collection of existing electron-light interaction models are not suitable for use in situations where the electron is rapidly moving.  We estimate a significant reduction in model count, potentially lowering the number from tens of millions to tens of thousands.  Ultimately, we believe that developing a narrower range of tight-binding models will greatly streamline their application in simulation of various phenomena across diverse fields including cosmology and quantum gravity, astrophysics and black holes, and laser applications.

In computer vision, obtaining precise 3D information from images is complicated due to various issues such as pose uncertainty, incomplete data, and corruption. Existing deep learning techniques often focus on utilising both 2D and 3D semantic keypoints in object detection and pose estimation tasks, but they fail to provide reliable results in such situations. We propose an innovative approach that combines a geometrically-consistent deep model with an algorithm rooted in classical methods to accurately calculate the pose of objects from images containing semantic keypoints. Our framework not only resists corruption but also provides an accurate representation of the scene by considering the spatial relationships between objects. Through extensive testing on a challenging dataset, our method has shown superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, demonstrating its robustness and reliability in object pose estimation tasks.

This research establishes methods for creating confidence intervals and squares for parameters of a Cauchy distribution that is shifted by a known value, denoted as $(\mu,\sigma^2)$, based on a sample of independent data. It is assumed that neither the location nor the scale parameter is known and are estimated using the sample mean and intermediate variance, which leads to a complex distribution with an irreducible parameter space of size 2. The paper shows that under a specific scaling of the parameters and distributions, both the estimated parameters and the predicted intervals/squares exhibit asymptotic independence and meet specified criteria. Additionally, the methods proposed for the Cauchy distribution share similarities with those previously developed for the normal distribution, with some distinct differences in implementation, computation, and theoretical validation. The research also involves extensive computational investigations that demonstrate the reliability and accuracy of the proposed methods, which are supported by numerical examples.

A new statistical method is developed for estimating sample sizes in basket trials with multiple disease subgroups, allowing for the sharing of information between subgroups during trial planning. This is accomplished through a Bayesian approach, where the trial designer incorporates a layer of uncertainty about subgroup effects using a non-informative prior on a common distribution for subgroup effects, resulting in accurate Bayesian confidence intervals for subgroup-specific treatment differences. This approach enables efficient trial planning by pooling resources and reducing required sample sizes. For a given level of error and desired power, our approach determines the minimum required sample sizes for each subgroup, comparing favorably to classical methods in terms of cost, with savings of 26-93% in one-sided tests and 11-85% in two-sided tests. The novel methodology is illustrated using actual data from a trial testing the efficacy of nivolumab in different types of cancers.

To meet the stringent requirements of high-precision motion systems in sensitive applications like microelectronics and astronomy, it is crucial to maintain a consistent and precise motion. However, mechanical motion systems are subject to variations in performance due to changes in their physical parameters, which can lead to performance degradation and errors unless addressed. Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) technology offers an effective approach to model and mitigate these effects, but its application to motion systems is less explored. This research investigates the application of LPV technology to a high-precision motion system, focusing on developing a model that can accurately capture the effects of parameter variations across different motion trajectories and use this information to improve the motion control, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in positioning errors.

Reconstructing a complete 3D model from partial point clouds is a crucial task in many applications, but directly aligning partial clouds is highly challenging due to distinct, usually unrelated, domains. Most existing methods focus on aligning a whole object to another whole object. Our work differs by aiming to align partial clouds to partial clouds. To address this issue, we propose a new approach, partial-to-partial alignment without needing complete 3D models. Our technique, PRNet, leverages a self-guided learning strategy by incorporating the input partial cloud as a guide for alignment. This guide enhances the alignment process by providing the guide net with valuable global context and allowing the regulator net to focus on relevant, localized features. By using partial clouds as the guide, our guide net and regulator net work together to generate a suitable 3D center for alignment. Subsequently, our projector net projects the guide net's 3D center onto the target partial cloud to determine the alignment position. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods. Additionally, we release their implementation and the corresponding dataset, part-net, for future research.

A group G has the R_infinity characteristic if it has an R_infinity sequence, which means there's a non-zero integer c such that for any non-zero integer b, the sequence of subgroups given by G / (Rad^b(G))^c tends to become identically equal to the trivial subgroup as b increases infinitely. In this paper, we prove that many nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups have the R_infinity characteristic. The paper further confirms that the R_infinity sequence of these groups is either eventually stationary or indefinitely growing. Additionally, the paper provides examples of solvable nilpotent Baumslag-Solitar groups that do not have the R_infinity characteristic, as well as establishes the R_infinity sequence for certain non-abelian nilpotent Baumslag-Solitar groups.

To evaluate the stability of the Standard Model, we compare the sensitivity capabilities of future high-energy colliders: a 27 TeV LHC-like collider, a 100 TeV HL-LHC, the ILC, the CLIC, a 100 TeV future circular collider, and the muon collider. The sensitivity is measured by the excluded mass, the coupling, and the fraction of the parameter space remaining uncertain. The results show that the stability of the Standard Model can be confirmed or ruled out at the next generation of colliders across a wide range of energy, except for the ILC, which cannot make a definitive decision at its planned energy, even with its advanced precision. The exclsuion capability of these future colliders can be optimized by building them at an energy that minimizes the exploration of the additional phase space, allowing for stronger constraints on new physics models.
