Recent breakthroughs in techniques such as time-resolved spectroscopy and dynamic electron density analysis have made it possible to obtain detailed insights into intricate chemical and biological processes. However, the conventional approach of treating dynamics as a means to explain observed properties tends to suffer from a lack of clear connections between cause and effect. This research introduces a novel method that uses optimization techniques to reverse-engineer time-dependent observations, yielding dynamic trajectories that accurately replicate those observed. By leveraging the wealth of knowledge contained within pre-trained machine-learning models, this method achieves exceptional performance, particularly for relatively small systems where explicit high-fidelity models are unavailable. This work has profound implications for reversing other types of time-resolved data, such as video footage or seismic records, and potentially transferring knowledge from simulation to experimental analysis.

We apply the resonance projection operator method to the quark model to derive ground state wave functions for $D^*$, $D^*_s$ resonances, then use this model to calculate density functions. Our model assumes a non-relativistic quark interaction consistent with QCD and results in system-wide wave functions satisfying the Faddeev equation system-wide. Our approach involves using an operator-valued density function, initially defined through the in-medium Bethe-Salpeter equation, then simplified using an operator-valued version of the resonance projection operator method. Our method involves projecting a Faddeev wave function associated with a quark and a light antiquark onto density functions of the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ resonances. Our calculations indicate that the wave functions for these particles are heavily distributed (at 70% to 80% strength) within the interior of the resonance. Our model also shows the density functions of these particles are primarily (at 80% to 90% strength) confined within a geometric interpretation of the resonance as a hard, spherical object. Our results in the meson momentum space align with those in the quark momentum space, indicating that the majority of the momentum is held by the quark (at 80% to 90% strength). Our model further suggests that the distribution of the quark and the light antiquark within the resonance is primarily static (at 80% to 90% strength). Our results

We investigate the property of non-regularity for Gelfand-Shilov spaces, $\Sigma_\sigma^\gamma$, for various cases, and provide counterexamples demonstrating that these spaces do not always exhibit non-regular properties. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the non-regular property is preserved under certain transformations. In addition, we examine the growth of Fourier functions within these spaces and relate our investigations to the behavior of Toeplitz operators, particularly in the context of ${\mathcal O}_M$. To support our analysis, we establish an essential lemma involving the bounds of mixed derivatives within ${\mathcal O}_M$.

Deep learning methods have achieved significant success in various computer vision tasks, but they often rely on labeled data, neglecting the fact that accessing perfect annotations can be costly and impractical. Moreover, over-reliance on labeled data makes trained models inflexible to changes in distribution within the training data set. To address these issues, our research focuses on developing a novel framework that generates high-quality labeled data on the fly for a given type of semantic segmentation task. This is made possible by a cycle-consistent GAN that exploits the inherent structure of semantic segmentation problems. As a result, our model can produce labeled data on the fly, eliminating the need for extensive data annotation, while also ensuring instance consistency through the use of a division loss. Ultimately, our approach enables the direct training of deep learning models on the entire unlabelled dataset without requiring any annotated data.

Our approach, RKLAD, is an advanced method for predicting the sequence of actions taken by a video game player by utilizing the concept of skill modules, which are intricate abilities exhibited by players. By applying a sophisticated kernel-based model to encode skills, we are able to train a deep neural network to predict the subsequent skill module sequence based on past actions and to assess the likelihood of subsequent action sequences given past behavior. Our method successfully addresses the issues of output sequence length and degree of branching, allowing for the calculation of accurate sequential probabilities in both cases. Experimental evaluations on data from the open-source Dota 2 dataset by the AI Research Group at the University of Technological Education of Athens in Greece demonstrated improved accuracy relative to baseline models.

A remarkable outburst known as the Superoutburst Blue Excess or Huge Eruption (SBBE) occurred in 1985 for the dwarf star AD Leo, resulting in a significant blue shift and increased luminosity. Observations of this event are of immense value for understanding the natural history of young active stars. Our research simulates the near-ultraviolet spectrum of AD Leo's outburst using a complex model that combines the effects of a cool outer atmosphere and a hot inner layer. By analyzing the spectral features and energy distribution, we identified the characteristics of these components and the extent of a boundary layer separating the outer and inner regions. Our analysis of the simulated spectrum and energy distribution indicates a good match with the observed data. Notably, the presence of a strong Fe XVI line in the simulated spectrum at the energy peak of 335 nm, which could be confirmed through future observations at higher resolution. Our model segments the energy distribution into a quasiblackbody component from the outer atmosphere, a hotter confiner, and a granular inner region. A comprehensive table presents the numerical values for each component and layer of the system, allowing for replication and modification of our results.

This research extends the method of deforming $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on almost $\mathrm{G}_2$-structures found in nearly-K$\rho$ structures to a broader class of such structures. A key focus is on how this method retains the link with the $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton deformed equation when the almost $\mathrm{G}_2$-structure becomes a nearly-K$\rho$ structure. Building on this method, we prove that any $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on an almost $\mathrm{G}_2$-structure deformed structure can be transformed into a $\mathrm{G}_2$-instanton on the original undeformed structure. This result is complemented by an investigation of the obstructions that arise when applying the method to simple connections.

This study expands on the work of Huang and Li by investigating C-normal weighted composition operators within the context of the Hardy space $H^2$. It involves verifying C-normality for specific operator families, establishing equivalent conditions with strict C-normality, and exploring connections to other related concepts. Additionally, two separate theorems are proven, one confirming that certain weighted composition operators are hyponormal, while the other establishes that a particular class of C-normal weighted composition operators is weakly power-bounded under specific conditions.

This paper delves into an extensive collection of $p'$-compositions with respect to prime numbers $p$, establishing a connection to random walks within the $n$-vertex additive residue graph. Notably, under the condition that $p$ does not divide $n$, extensive compositions can be shown to have a statistical distribution where a significant proportion, if any, have distinct walk paths. This finding is based on an in-depth analysis of the walk's local structure and its spectral properties.

We introduce the Basic Oriented Point representation, a versatile method for encoding spatial awareness in machine learning models, and address the issue of noise in this representation by developing an unbiased smoothing technique called Transformation-Dependent Point Cloud (TPC) smoothing. TPC can be applied at both the input and feature representation levels. Our experiments show that TPC effectively reduces noise in point cloud datasets and improves the performance of downstream tasks using cleaned data. Additionally, TPC is capable of accelerating inference times in downstream tasks.

This research investigates the performance of ALOHA and CSMA using frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar networks, focusing on medium access control (MAC). ALOHA, being a simple protocol, transmits data whenever a node is ready, whereas a node in a CSMA network only transmits after detecting that the channel is clear. Contrary to traditional views, that ALOHA generates too much traffic and CSMA saves the channel, this study reveals that ALOHA's performance is comparable to CSMA in radar-specific environments. A model is developed to calculate the probability of two or more active transmitters due to repeated successful transmissions from multiple nodes. In addition to this, derived expressions for second moments of key parameters in radar networks are included in the study. This work is further extended to optimize ALOHA parameters statistically. Results show that ALOHA and CSMA have similar probabilities of cochannel interference, that ALOHA is optimal when retransmission probabilities equal success probabilities, and that CSMA is merely a specialized case of ALOHA with reduced transmission rates. Moreover, theoretical predictions are confirmed through empirical analyses.

Recent studies using entangled two-photon physics have leveraged Hong-Ommandel interference to explore various concepts in quantum optics, although a detailed analysis of the involved photon absorption effects has yet to be presented in this work. Utilizing a recognized unit for quantifying optical losses, a detailed examination of these losses is conducted for both linear and nonlinear scenarios. Moreover, this work discusses the implications of utilizing entangled two-photon absorption for exploring novel optical materials while also highlighting the distinctions between optical losses resulting from this process and those caused by conventional irradiation.

We show in this paper that a dimension-independent form of complex projective space cohomology can be obtained through calculating the logical circle equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex vector spaces. This results from applying the extended Zompro functor to the elliptic cohomology theory based on the simr principle. We also derive the equivariant elliptic cohomology theory based on the simr principle when the group of equivariance is the logical circle, and subsequently express complex projective space cohomology in terms of the simr theory by computing the extended Zompro functor. This applies to cohomology across various dimensions and in different forms. The derivation involves the application of T-duality to derive the cohomology rings of complex projective spaces of V when the dimension of V is greater than or equal to two. We also express 2-dimensional complex projective spaces cohomology in terms of generators a and b using the simr theory, and demonstrate that the deformed cohomology theory based on the simr principle is capable of reflecting O(2)-equivariance. This means the elliptic cohomology theory based on the simr principle is equipped with the O(2)-equivariance, which is fundamental to T-duality. The final step in this paper is the application of the extended Zompro functor to the simr theory to generate the logical circle equivariance, and the resulting expression of complex projective space cohomology in terms of the

Knowledge graph completion, specifically temporal knowledge graph inference, has gained interest for enhancing knowledge graphs with missing information. Many approaches have been attempted to date. This research focuses on a low-rank and model-independent representation method for temporal knowledge graph inference, aiming to flexibly represent entities and relationships within the given context. It also introduces a flexible sampling strategy for transfer learning to adapt to various entity types. The evaluation showed that this approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods when applied to Wikidata, achieving superior results across multiple metrics.

A common issue in audio applications involves removing noisy background sounds known as ground noise. A new type of ground noise is introduced in this study which, unlike commonly used methods, is both non-stationary and spatially coherent. The experiment uses recordings from twin microphones on a moving camera to capture sound, revealing that current noise reduction techniques struggle when confronted with this type of noise. A unique method utilizing a camera's motion model is proposed to distinguish between the useful audio and the new type of ground noise. The technique relies on the assumption that the source of the ground noise remains relatively static. While the source of the camera motion is known, the approach does not require any prior knowledge. The technique can work with existing recording equipment and is tested using a capsule microphone on a camera, demonstrating positive results in removing the new type of ground noise and improving audio focus.

Despite the prevalence of Bell nonlocality, demonstrating its absolute form remains elusive. This study aims to alleviate that challenge by creating an instance of perfect Bell nonlocality using specific types of quantum states and their non-transformable properties. We establish a non-transformable non-local correlation, meaning it cannot be replicated through any deterministic process based on shared randomness, by constructing a specific set of measurement outcomes. This correlation is derived from a particular kind of entanglement, ensuring its non-locality cannot be explained through any deterministic or probabilistic scenario based on shared randomness. Additionally, this study also examines the non-locality of other correlation types, including those from quantum circuit-based non-locality, which often rely on specific assumptions such as the ability to conduct measurements or communicate efficiently. This work combines elements of such studies to provide a more comprehensive understanding of non-locality, offering new insights and perspectives on the topic.

Flat bands are bands with zero density of states at the Fermi level, yet they are not inherently stable. In this study, flat bands are confined in a pseudo-periodic box and their confinement is quantified to demonstrate that all flat bands are confining. Confinement induces a negative shift in the band structure, causing the emergence of a non-flat band as a result of a self-consistent calculation. This research provides a systematic explanation for the origin of flat bands in a wide range of systems through a simple model, thus offering a new perspective on flat bands and confinement.

Researchers are eager to learn if and how superconductivity works in basic hydrogen compounds, like MB2 (where M is a metal), because of their unique electronic properties and behavioral patterns. This has led to a flurry of experiments trying to create and studying these substances, and simulations have shown that they can display remarkable properties. However, we found that hydrogen boride does not become a superconductor, and our research explains why. We found that the local structure of hydrogen boride is quite different from predicted models used in theoretical calculations, which affects the results significantly. By using experimental data as a starting point, we found that hydrogen boride does not have the characteristics required for it to be a superconductor.

A C C C implements execute (also known as emit) behavior for C G S 'happen-before' relationships, providing a fundamental aspect of the programming model, which is based on 'happen-before'. This specification defines the essential characteristics of an C G S 'happen-before' based on happen-before events, establishes the criteria for a correct happen-before implementation, and serves as a framework for testing such an happen-before. This document also serves as a testing framework for an happen-before, which can be used to evaluate the performance of different happen-before optimisation techniques.

We introduce two new concepts, charmability and rigidity, for finitely generated groups. Our findings reveal that (1) only finitely presented groups with certain exponential growth are characterizable through charmable presentations, while (2) groups exhibiting rigidity are both characterizable through unique presentations and have exponential growth. Additionally, our research demonstrates that (3) a group's rigidity implies its charmability, and (4) a group's unique characterizability implies its rigidity. We further establish that (5) arithmetic groups with associated number field transfer functions are both characterizable and rigid.

Highly automated vehicles require rapid and reliable responses to unexpected events to prevent accidents and ensure safe operation. The automotive industry adopts fail-safe designs by incorporating redundant systems that operate in conjunction to guarantee system reliability in case of component failure. Nevertheless, this conservative approach might not always be necessary, and more efficient strategies could be possible if the proper mathematical framework and tools are applied. For instance, fail-functioning designs, where systems continue to operate safely though not at full capacity, might be feasible. However, proving the validity of such designs poses significant theoretical challenges. In this research, we tackle these issues by developing an advanced formal model for system safety, incorporating features of fail-functioning designs. Furthermore, we utilize symbolic model checking to verify the integrity of our system design from start to completion. The proposed methodology is demonstrated using a practical case study based on a simplified vehicle control system.

In this work, we develop an innovative framework for classifying dynamical systems using their response profiles, which are derived from brief and non-invasive perturbations. This approach is particularly applicable to studying complex systems with multiple dynamics and abrupt changes, such as those found in climate and neural dynamics. Our system can also identify and analyze multiple switching points within a single system, whose identification is currently hampered by a lack of effective methods. By employing impact-based clustering, we can obtain clustered groups whose members are highly similar and the system's behavior transitions abruptly between, thus providing valuable insights into complex systems. Our method is demonstrated using two practical case studies, one involving a simple mathematical model and another based on real-world data.

This study develops a modern interpretation of Leibnizian infinitesimal analysis, incorporating concepts from both a general topological space setting and specific theories of intervals and second-order dense metric spaces. To establish this analysis, we built upon the foundational ideas expressed in Leibniz's writings, adopting a modern perspective. Our work is primarily an organizational effort, synthesizing existing research and presenting it in a comprehensive manner. In the process, we necessarily included some minor theoretical extensions.

Using interferometric data from HI intensity mapping experiments, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the large-scale structure of the Universe, despite the redshift distortion that affects accuracy. Our analysis presents an extended model that describes the distortion's impact on interferometric data and accounts for the removal of background signals. This improved model enables more accurate predictions compared to the standard "geodesic approximation," allowing for higher precision at large scales. Our findings also reveal that the effects of disturbance theory, or "shell corrections," are minimal at small to moderate scales but become more significant at scales greater than 20 Mpc^3. Our analysis further identifies the source of an apparent disagreement between simulations and observations of the large-scale structure, suggesting that the use of interferometric data may not be perfectly aligned with the requirements of cosmological principle.

A significant shift occurs in how we perceive freedom and uncontrolled growth when considering complex systems with inherent organizational structure. In the context of selection theory, autonomy refers to a type of operativity where an element or system can be represented by a finite number of coefficients, operating on a potentially infinite-dimensional space. This unique perspective reveals that freedom and uncontrolled growth share certain underlying similarities. For instance, just as uncontrolled growth in a complex system often manifests as an exponential increase in dimensions, autonomy does so through an infinite series of extensions in infinite-dimensional spaces. Exploring the concept of autonomy leads to a deeper examination of uncontrolled growth, particularly in relation to Riccati equations, which sheds new light on R. R. Stöckler's celebrated theorem. This analysis reveals that freedom and uncontrolled growth are intertwined concepts, as well as different forms of operativity, which are interconnected.

One issue with recommender systems is data sparsity, causing incomplete user-item rating matrices. Researchers have developed various techniques to address this problem, including using external data sources or combining multiple approaches. However, the approach taken by Guo et al. in 2019 is unique in that it focuses on merging context-driven and behavior-driven methods. This system first employs KDD Cup 2011 movie data and Mahout to build a hybrid model by combining two key techniques: collaborative filtering and content-based methods. The proposed method leverages document context-driven recommendations, based on users' historical behavior, to overcome the limitations of traditional CF methods. The experiment revealed a hybrid score for each recommended item, consisting of two parts: one from the relevant but uninteracted content based on users' behavior, and another from the rated but unvisited items' ratings. This score effectively balances exploration and exploitation, leading to improved performance across three evaluation metrics.

Wang and Zhou introduced a concept of freeness, referred to as "freeness of kind B", as an extension to non-commutative stochastic processes, where a direct link can be established between this extension and the concept of conditional independence in non-commutative probability theory. In this research, we aim to extend the concept of freeness of kind B to random matrices, where a sufficient condition for determining the freeness of kind B of both row and column spaces of certain classes of random matrices, particularly the GUE, has been found. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the matrix-valued non-commutative stochastic processes formed through diagonalization of random matrices do not exhibit freeness of kind B, although they may satisfy other criteria for freeness. This research also explores the relationship between the spectral distribution of non-commutative stochastic processes and their freeness of kind B.

For model-checking purposes, adding time constraints to state spaces often yields favorable results. A notable method involves using timed graphs, which can be derived from timed transition systems by discretizing time into separate units. However, the addition of time constraints leads to an exponential increase in state spaces. To mitigate this issue, the authors investigate under which conditions this exponential growth can be avoided. They achieve this goal by reducing the base state space and ensuring that time constraints do not exponentially increase the state spaces. Two specific scenarios are provided where these conditions can be met: when the underlying transition system has a bounded transition density and when the underlying transition system has a finite number of states.

Our objective is to explore the connection between $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ through meson transition form factors, which are computed using a fully dynamical calculation at the $q^2 \to 0$ limit via an effective method. To this end, we define a set of reference processes, namely $\gamma^* \to Q \bar Q$ and $\pi^0 \to \gamma \eta$, and derive the form factors for $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ by combining these with the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ intermolecular. We observe that the form factors for these processes exhibit the same behavior with respect to the momentum of the meson, which is dedicated to the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ intermolecular. Additionally, we calculate the partial decay widths of the decay $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and note that they conform to the theoretical predictions based on the vector dominance model. Conversely, the decay widths of the process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ cannot be explained through the vector dominance model, which indicates

The GRAVITY instrument on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) employs a capture camera to enable a broad-field view, which facilitates the alignment of its ten single-dish images into a seamless, high-resolution picture.  Two distinct approaches were used to determine the orientation of these images, known as the "Gamma-method" and the "POLY method", respectively.  Both techniques effectively verifiably identify the correct capture camera image alignment within large collections of interferometric images.  Furthermore, both approaches accurately determine the VLTI sub-system orientations, which were then utilized to refine the capture camera's geometry, thus enabling the calibration of GRAVITY's high-resolution images.  Two distinct capture cameras were utilized: the original was based on an 1kx1k CCD device, while the upgraded version utilized the VAINA camera, which features an array of four e2V CCD devices combining to form a 2kx2k sensitivity equivalent sensitivity.  Following the instrument's upgrade in 2018, the capture camera was replaced with the VAINA device, which exhibited improved sensitivity and a broader field of view.  Nonetheless, both capture cameras successfully contributed to the determination of GRAVITY's high-resolution image orientation and sub-system orientations, which were then utilized to define the reference frame for the VLTI baseline orientations.  Consequently, the capture camera's data played a critical role in the ongoing calibration of VLTI's baseline orientations.

We examine the $k$-Center problem in the doubling metric space and observe that it differs significantly from the problem in highway metric space. While an polynomial time approximation algorithm exists for the latter, it is known to be hard to achieve any approximation in the former, even in doubling space. We investigate the $k$-Center problem in the generalized highway network, where the underlying graph only requires an (8k+1)-doubling property, and provide a constant ratio approximation algorithm for the first time. We achieve this result by employing a new FTSP approximation technique and obtaining an FTSP instance with (8k+1)-doubling property, for any given k.

This paper builds upon previous research by Xu and Li, extending their findings under altered criteria related to the $b$-$f$ shift difference. Furthermore, we offer counterexamples to demonstrate that certain outcomes cannot be achieved when the $b$-$f$ shift difference does not adhere to specific requirements.

This research presents a novel, efficient approach to solving polynomial linear systems with random errors. By building on the probabilistic approach of Papadopoulou and Song, our algorithm offers enhanced performance, achieving a lower number of required operations. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of an early cessation condition to reduce computation time. To demonstrate the correctness of our approach, we provide formal proofs of boundedness and solve the problem within a specified time limit. The algorithm's efficiency is measured in terms of arithmetic operations and memory accesses. Our experimental results confirm that the new approach outperforms the existing probabilistic method, yielding a significant speedup of up to 40 times. Moreover, the early cessation condition adds an additional 10-20% speedup.

In two-dimensional systems where parity symmetry is breached, a unique phenomenon known as bundle emission occurs, where a single electron emits two particles instead of one. We are studying this effect in a zigzag edge state of an elementary moiré Haldane model, where the broken parity symmetry causes the emergence of chiral bundle photons. To confirm our theory, we performed exact diagonalization on a finite cluster and examined the bundle photon emission rates, which showed that they cannot be explained by a semi-classical model. However, the electron's interaction with two transverse photons follows a specific set of rules, governing the emission of left- and right-circularly polarized photons. As a result, the bundle photon emission of one edge state is mirrored as an emission of two photons from the other edge state, displaying opposing circular polarization. This relationship holds even at high electron energies but fails for edge states with preserved parity symmetry, where the bundle photon emission disappears while the emission of individual photons persists.

A precise and straightforward analytical model is presented to describe the thermodynamic behavior of a pure alkali gas in equilibrium. This model effectively captures the unique characteristics of each alkali element, depending on their atomic mass and nuclear properties. It is noteworthy that this model achieves exceptional precision at high temperatures, surpassing the accuracy of the widely accepted Saha equation, particularly for certain elements where the assumptions behind the Saha equation may not hold true.

In the context of a medium with a specific type of matter, we investigate how vector mesons interact and are influenced by the interaction. The presence of a medium creates a difference between the vector mesons' actions and their currents, which has significant implications. The internal structure of the vector mesons, particularly their behavior in response to a external electric field, is examined using two different theoretical frameworks. One approach utilizes calculations based on the Wigner-Eckart theorem, while the other framework relies on a theoretical model that incorporates the concept of chiral discrepancy. Through these analyses, the concept of form factors becomes crucial and we calculate these form factors within the context of the chiral discrepancy model. The results of our study, particularly the impact of the chiral discrepancy, on the internal structure of the vector mesons, especially their reaction to an external electric field, are significant and have important implications for understanding particle physics.

We are studying a unique distributed estimation challenge where a large network of nodes comes together to calculate a global property of the network itself. While each node has access to local information, we are focusing on a specific distribution algorithm that works well even in the presence of malicious nodes. We are examining a set of established estimation problems, including graph diameter, average degree, and graph conductance. We have developed the first-ever scalable and efficient algorithms for these problems, even when the network is complex and large. We have also studied the minimum requirements necessary to solve these problems efficiently. Interestingly, we found that the impact of malicious nodes can significantly slow down some algorithms, but not others. This distinction applies especially to estimating graph diameter, which is sensitive to the presence of malicious nodes.

In numerical relativity, the Conformal Transverse Traceless gauge is widely used for reducing computational complexity, especially when dealing with higher-order perturbations and coarse-graining techniques. However, the CTTK approach falls apart when there's no a clear choice for a background conformal metric. Our method resolves this issue by adopting a more relaxed approach to data restrictions, allowing for the use of a transient conformal metric that can vary with time. We demonstrate that this approach leads to comparable accuracy in the computed wave patterns compared to the standard method. Since the CTTK approach only restricts transverse traceless components of the metric, it remains consistent with the constraints obtained from the standard method, especially in the regions far away from the source. The source's residual non-conformal and transverse traceless components are accurately identified and stored as residual degrees of freedom. This work has important implications for the development of optimized numerical methods in relativity.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves determining the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough examination of over 20,000 20-inch PMTs. This study outlines the detailed examination procedures used to assess the properties of these PMTs, including a 1/m rating system to evaluate their dark noise, which proved to be a reliable method for predicting the PMTs' quality. The final selection of 20,000 20-inch PMTs exceeded the experiment's initial targets, with more than 90% of the selected PMTs featuring exceptional performance.

In practical scenarios like power grid forecasting and traffic forecasting, long-term predictions are often required, but current models have limitations when it comes to accurately forecasting beyond a few hours or days. To address this challenge, a new model called LongSTN is proposed, which can predict for extended periods of time by incorporating an advanced spatio-temporal forecasting component. The proposed model, LongSTN, integrates a deep learning-based forecasting method with an advanced graph convolutional neural network, allowing it to account for complex relationships in space and time. The model's structure is adaptively configured to optimize forecasting performance, and experiments demonstrate its superior performance compared to leading benchmark models.

Deep space observations are obstructed by Earth's atmosphere, posing solutions to mitigate its scattering effects. Through on-sky observations, we study the scattering effect in various atmospheric models, identifying three distinct phases as necessary for mitigating scattering. By characterizing these models, we can determine the best approach to apply them in real-world observations, whether in real-time or via post-processing, to effectively reduce scattering effect.

Educational datasets labeled by multiple instructors can vary greatly in quality due to differing labels resulting from conflicting interpretations of data. To address this, we develop PILE, an innovative distillation method that utilizes multiple instructors' varying expertise effectively. PILE employs a coalition formation approach based on iterative pairwise iterations, where each iteration identifies a cohesive group of instructors producing the most accurate combined labels for a dataset. During distillation, PILE updates model logits by taking an average of the group's combined labels at each iteration. PILE's iterative coalition formation and logit averaging approach seamlessly integrate the diversity of instructors and produce highly accurate distilled labels. Notably, our experiments demonstrate that PILE, using only three instructors, can replicate the accuracy of a solo, highly experienced instructor, while also producing more robust models against adversarial attacks.

In systems where the interaction between dark matter and normal matter is strong, large-recoil events may be followed by emitting high-energy photons as a result of the relaxation of dark matter overdensities, known as dark matter emittings. This process could appear similar to the decay of dark matter particles, potentially leading to similar outcomes in dark matter searches, such as incorrect conclusions about the dark matter particle mass and interaction strength. This wrong impression could then lead to incorrect interpretations of other experimental observations related to dark matter. This phenomenon could be observed using nuclear-recoil experiments that measure low momentum transfers, as well as using optical detectors sensitive to birefringence and anisotropy. Dark matter emittings can be distinguished from particle decays through differences in their properties, such as the frequency of signal occurrence, light scattering properties, and the relationship between energy and momentum. This distinction can be utilized to identify ultra-light dark matter particles, which cannot be detected through direct particle searches. This process could provide valuable insights into the properties of ultra-light dark matter particles.

This paper explores the recovery of sparse signals given noisy measurements, focusing on a particular optimization method. Unlike previous studies, we do not place restrictions on the number of non-zero coefficients, and instead, we aim to find a solution with the fewest coefficients. Under specific conditions, we establish that a unique solution exists and prove it can be calculated efficiently.

P4 has gained widespread acceptance as a flexible programming language for networking hardware, allowing programmers to efficiently create custom switch architectures. A versatile compiler for P4 is crucial as it enables users to translate P4 programs into suitable hardware or simulation environments. Despite the existence of multiple commercial P416 compilers, there is a lack of suitable open-source alternatives. Our proposal addresses this gap by introducing an open-source P416 compiler framework, which utilizes the MaxPlus2 syntax and is compatible with P4.org-compliant programs. This versatile compiler can translate P4 programs into a flexible, adjustable match-action table-based architecture. The resulting architecture can be optimized and tailored to fit various network processing requirements using knobs at different levels of the protocol stack. Our open-source compiler has already shown great results in producing efficient P4 programs, particularly when compared to commercial alternatives.

In this work, we focus on discretising the vector conveyance equation using the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements. A novel, enhanced discretisation of this variable-diffusion equation is presented, implemented using a mixed finite element approach. It's observed that the standard and a previously proposed discrete methods suffer from suboptimal spatial error convergence when using the RT elements. In contrast, the new approach achieves an optimal $h^2$ convergence rate for solutions with smooth enough spatial variation. Additionally, we examine the time-dependent conveyance equation, applying both the Galerkin and Balakrishnan-Loinger time-stepping methods. For the former, a slightly modified approach is required to achieve a $k^{-1}$ convergence rate in time, while the BLP method yields an optimal $k^{-1/2}$ convergence rate. Several numerical examples confirm the theoretical predictions, demonstrating that the new approach outperforms the standard and a previously proposed methods in terms of precision.

The ground truth for fair distributed training is complex, consisting of multiple layers of fairness enforcement and data sensitivity.  Federated Learning can partially fulfill this requirement by accommodating Justice constraints, but its ability to meet Differential Confidentiality constraints remains uncertain.  DL encounters two novel concepts, Differential Privacy and Kerckhoffs' Principle, to bridge the gap between Federated Learning and cryptographic protocols for encrypted training.  The resulting theoretical framework allows for the derivation of privacy guarantees from Federated Learning hyperparameters, providing a new perspective on the field.  Empirical testing has confirmed the theoretical predictions, establishing a connection between Federated Learning and the Security Games framework.  The integration of Differential Privacy and Federated Learning proves to be robust, but its combined effect is less secure than previously thought (specifically, up to 250 times less secure).  A new optimization algorithm is introduced to mitigate this security breach by finding the best balance between utility and privacy.  The novel approach is generalizable to other encrypted training methods, offering a flexible framework for application.  The developer of the DL framework can select various training protocols, such as Homomorphic Logistic Regression, in order to achieve the desired privacy level, leveraging the introduced theoretical framework for evaluation and comparison.

The $B_c^+$ meson, comprised of a quark with equal parts charm and bottom, has been of considerable interest in the study of heavy light mesons due to its unique composition. Although it was first observed in 1980, there have been ongoing debates about its discovery ever since. The main goal of this study is to investigate the existence of a stimulated $B_c^+$ state with the quantum numbers of $I^G(1/2^+)$ that consists of the $B_c^+\to J/\psi \pi^+$ decay. Using a relativistic quark model, the study computed the transition form factor and decay rate of the $B_c^+\to J/\psi \pi^+$ process within the framework of perturbative QCD. The calculated transition form factor was then compared to experimental data from the BESIII collaboration, and as a result, the study found that the calculated results satisfactorily explain the observed peaks in two spectra. The study's findings provide significant evidence for the observation of a stimulated $B_c^+$ state.

Inspired by recent advancements in Continuous-Phase Cramer-Rao Bound analysis, 
we introduce the Continuous-Phase Runge-Kutta method for solving differential equations 
with a novel estimator that achieves nearly optimal performance, 
even in the presence of significant noise and unknown parameters. 
This approach can be applied to various estimation problems involving differential equations, 
such as tracking the position of a pendulum or a free fall object, 
which is illustrated through multiple simulations in noisy scenarios.

When training neural networks, sending data to the main computing unit can create significant communication bottlenecks that hinder the process. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in model-parallel training for deep models. To mitigate this issue, we have developed a novel approach which distributes the workload across multiple computing units with their own memory to speed up training. Our method involves splitting the main model into distinct components and training them separately. Although these components are learning the same model, they are working with different views of the data due to a special algorithm that shuffles the information. This, combined with the fact that we send data to the main computing unit only when it's absolutely necessary, has significantly reduced communication costs. Furthermore, we have found that regional evaluators can be trained independently to assess the model's performance without consolidating information first. This has led to a significant reduction in evaluation costs and allowed us to use more complex models. Our approach has been successfully validated by applying it to the ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 models.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart, despite being relatively less explored. Recent research has extended this area of study by investigating how a non-uniform electrical field affects 3D chaotic scattering in the case of the standard three-dimensional kicked Hamiltonian. The results show that in the absence of dissipation, this system exhibits Wada basins characteristic of self-repelling attractors. However, introducing minimal dissipation has a surprising effect - it enhances and strengthens the Wada basins in the parameter range associated with stable periodic orbits. Conversely, in the parameter range associated with unbound motion, dissipation causes the formation of three-dimensional 'whirlpools' that trap particles, thereby reducing the available phase space and affecting scattering dynamics. The study finds that dissipation can significantly impact 3D chaotic scattering, particularly through the appearance of new transmission phases, and sheds light on the universal characteristics of dissipative systems above the 2D threshold, potentially leading to further generalizations in the field.

Variations in the standard model's electroweak sector could lead to the creation of a new type of force-mediated interaction that affects quark flavor, which in turn has significant implications for the creation of matter-antimatter pairs at the LHC. To understand the behavior of this new interaction, it's necessary to define its duration, which in turn helps to clarify its consistency with existing observations. To explain the stability of ordinary matter without producing excessive antimatter, the duration of this interaction is restricted. Finally, the possibility of this new interaction aligning with the principles of naturalness in particle physics is explored.

In daily life, people frequently encounter a vast amount of activity data, and it's a challenging task to recognize them due to inconsistent lighting, obstructions, and limited snippet lengths. Current methods apply fully focused techniques such as C3D and LSTM to make up for the lack of data, but they don't suit rare activities and often result in low accuracy. We propose an HiFocus network, a two-layered approach that combines a focused focus network for rare activity recognition and a de-focused focus network for general tasks. The de-focused focus network incorporates efficient features from a self-attention module and uses transition layers and average pooling to achieve optimal results. The HiFocus network leverages a data augmentation technique to compensate for data shortages in rare activities. The de-focused focus network employs a hybrid transition layer to effectively capture key information from adjacent frames. Experimental results on NTU-RGB+D, Kinetics, and HMDB51 datasets demonstrate the superior performance of HiFocus over state-of-the-art models.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship hypothesis in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes with a scalar field is crucial for understanding black hole physics. Our research into the thermodynamics of these black holes reveals that they adhere to the extended first law and Euler theorem. Moreover, we analyzed the cosmic censorship hypothesis by examining the variation of the mass and scalar curvature in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes. Our findings suggest that this hypothesis holds true for the majority of initial parameters. However, almost all violations occur within a specific, very small range of initial parameters where the scalar field's magnitude is minimal. Importantly, we discovered that none of these parameters lead to minimal black hole formation.

According to the chemical evolution model, heavy elements were primarily created through massive stellar events. Yet, a notable discrepancy exists between predicted light levels from primitive stars and the expected levels based on this stellar model, suggesting either the stellar mechanism is flawed or a non-stellar explanation exists for the genesis of heavy elements. A possible flaw in the stellar model has prompted consideration of an alternative, namely that the progenitors of these stars were not nuclearly primordial. It is proposed that a significant portion of these stars initially consisted of light isotopes of silicon and magnesium, which were formed by the operation of the C-fusion process in an early generation of stars. The unusual configurations of these early stars are attributed to the characteristics of the Rosetta reaction, which describes how elements under going nuclear transformation in a stellar environment retain their initial elemental identity. The hypothesis that the unusual initial conditions of these stars were governed by the Rosetta reaction, which mediates cosmic nucleosynthesis, is dubbed the Rosetta Model.

This paper presents a new method to estimate thermodynamic quantities and their variations, using Nested Sampling as a Bayesian approach. We demonstrate that NS has inherent capabilities for computing these quantities, which are closely tied to the concept of differential entropy. Our proposal aligns with the principles of Quantum Field Theory, where entropy is seen as a fundamental thermodynamic quantity. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, we apply it to calculate the entropy and specific heat of a simple non-relativistic quantum gas.

This research focuses on a specific type of conservation law that is non-linear in nature. It can be viewed as a extension of the classical Lax-Friedrics-Shock principle, with the usual solutions enhanced to include a measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A key aspect of this work is the identification of feeble solutions, which are related to a specific variational framework, leveraging the structure of the mapping that underpins the problem. Building on existing theories for single equations, it is shown that feeble solutions form a continuous and stable solution relative to initial data in the $L^2$ norm. Importantly, it is demonstrated that feeble solutions are not necessarily bounded in the $L^\infty$ norm. Consequently, this analysis raises questions about whether these solutions are indeed solutions of a measure-valued type, which is confirmed through an indirect approach. A new class of feeble solutions is defined and it is proven that they are equivalent to the exact solutions of the conservation laws.

Cyberattacks on IoT devices and networks continue to evolve at a rapid pace, 
withening threats extending to the world's most critical infrastructure. As these 
attacks have far-reaching consequences for society, there is an ever-increasing 
need for timely and effective threat detection. To address this need, a new system 
is proposed that uses time-series data from network traffic to classify assault types 
in real-time. This system, relying solely on Naive Bayes and time-series encoding, 
delivers accurate assault classification across various complex scenarios. With its 
compact size and lack of sophisticated features, Naive Bayes and time-series encoding 
are an ideal combination for resource-constrained devices, providing fast and efficient 
threat detection. This flexibility positions Naive Bayes and time-series encoding 
as a versatile solution, also effective in larger deployments, for use in hardware 
or software form.

Let $G$ be a solvable finite group that has at least two elements. We define the expansion of the group $G$ as the smallest number of subsets that contain more elements than $G$ itself when the union of these subsets has fewer elements than the original group. In this paper, we provide an exact calculation of the expansion of solvable groups in various cases and offer a general upper limit on the expansion for any solvable group $G$, which is given by $\log_2{(o(G))/2}$ if $G$ is not simple, or by $\log_2{(o(G))/1}$ if $G$ is simple. Additionally, we propose several conjectures about the expansion of solvable groups, which are supported by the results obtained for specific types of solvable groups.

In this work, we have developed an algorithm to detect the movement of plants and animals in video captured in a natural, outdoor setting. The research is part of a broader project that involves using computer technology to monitor and study ecological systems. Although the algorithm used in this work is specifically designed to process data from cameras positioned in outdoor environments, it is also applicable to a number of other tasks including medical imaging and video analytics. The methodology employed involves applying a unique mathematical formula to eliminate the background pattern from the video, and then using optical character recognition techniques to identify the remaining moving entities. The project researchers are interested in using this algorithm to help with segmentation tasks in natural, outdoor video footage.

To address the contemporary issue of limited energy supply, we propose utilizing quantum finitude to augment the capacity of energy networks. We present a quantum formula that can be applied to both existing and newly constructed power plants to determine their energy output. We demonstrate the necessity of using quantum methods in calculations due to the large values of electric charge and Planck's constant involved. The methodology of our study is to first outline a general framework for quantum energy production, and then verify our approach through the analysis of a simplified model representing a combined power of two sources (nuclear and fossil fuel) before being scaled up to a more comprehensive model.

Our objective is to examine how underlying physical laws might relate to the overall structure of the world's information content. We begin with a general principle that the flow of information should conform to predictable patterns, thereby allowing us to identify irregularities in the universe's information profile. Utilizing the concept of entropy, we explore the concept of "information darkness," which serves as a four-dimensional counterpart to the traditional concept of darkness in two-dimensional surfaces. By applying the Riemann-Hurwitz formula, we calculate the amount of "darkness" present within the universe's larger structure, thereby estimating the extent of inconsistencies in the universe's overall information content. This approach is applied to both quantum mechanics and general relativity, with quantum mechanics revealing a peaking of entropy beyond the Planck scale and general relativity indicating consistent behavior throughout the cosmos.

A comprehensive search in high-energy proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider is presented, focusing on heavy, long-lived particles that interact with quarks and other particles in a specific way. This search utilized the ATLAS experiment's entire dataset collected in 2015-2018, recording collisions at a 13 TeV energy level with a total exposure of 139 inverse femtobarns. Investigating a wide range of possible masses and lifetimes, the analysis examines the phenomenon of energy loss due to ionisation in a specific detector component. As a result, the search sets new standards for Standard Model boundaries and provides constraints on hypothetical particles with various properties, including a massive Z-like particle, a pair of W-like particles, and other exotic entities.

We have developed a highly efficient on-chip single-photon device based on a silicon carbide material, which is designed for use in ridge waveguides and has a central wavelength of 1625 nm. The device generates highly tunable, near-resonant photons via a two-level system, utilizing a combination of electrical and optical stimulation. The conversion efficiency of our on-chip single-photon generator is exceptional, at 76%, due in part to the use of a highly effective parameter for optical stimulation, which surpasses currently available generators based on silicon and quantum dots. This high efficiency will greatly benefit the integration of quantum computing systems, allowing for the seamless addition of high-performance single-photon devices to existing optical networks.

Neutron spin echo spectroscopy was used to investigate the dynamics of a nearly pure boson system in its superfluid and condensed states. By applying successive heat treatments to a $^4$He-filled cylindrical container within a beamline instrument, researchers were able to study the system's thermal and molecular evolution. The technique allowed for the measurement of the complex modulated structure factor $S(q,\omega)$, which gave valuable insights into the formation and movement of heat cumulants within the boson summit. The observed change in $q$-dependent relaxation processes was consistent with expectations from theoretical models of boson kinetics. The study demonstrated that neutron spin echo can be an effective tool for investigating early stages of boson condensation and superfluidity.

Particle physics precision is limited by theoretical and experimental errors, with theoretical errors stemming from incomplete calculational methods. Specifically, the self-energy integrals of heavy particles, such as the tauon, are challenging to calculate exactly and pose a problem for accuracy in related phenomena. Although there has been significant progress in understanding these integrals with arbitrary IR divergences through differential equations, the problem persists for finite, but small, masses. This work addresses this challenge by breaking down the self-energy integral into simpler components, evaluating a base integral with a novel approach and using known results for additional components. The proposed method is adaptable to various loop configurations and can be applied to different particles. Additionally, this approach makes it easier to identify and isolate IR divergences, facilitating a more straightforward implementation of sector decomposition in numerical evaluation. As a proof of concept, this work provides a numerical evaluation of the polarized $\tau$ hadronic decay using this new method.

The ability of disordered materials to absorb and process energy is heavily influenced by the presence of pathways or channels that transfer energy from one part of the system to another. To uncover these pathways in scattering systems without prior knowledge, we developed a method to automatically identify them by analyzing the system's responses to various external influences. To confirm our findings, we proved that the total energy absorbed by the system must be distributed evenly across all identified pathways. Furthermore, we discovered that the total energy absorbed by the system is limited by the number of these pathways and must be greater than or equal to the number of unidirectional pathways in the system. These conclusions are applicable to both coherent and non-coherent energy absorption processes.

Researchers have spent decades studying the inner 10,000 light-years of the Milky Way, yet a particular spiral feature, known as the 3-kpc 362 MHz HI cloud, has remained puzzling due to its enigmatic position and possible identity. A new study offers a fresh analysis of the cloud's characteristics, derived from data from the HIJASS survey, the VLA Galactic Plane Survey, and the APOGEE-2 project. By comparing these values with current models of the Milky Way, researchers find a pattern of gas densities and velocities that suggests the cloud shares the Galaxy's rotation. Furthermore, it's determined that the cloud is an offshoot of the nearby spiral arm, distinguishable from the distinct 4-kpc Ring by its weaker density and larger opening angle. It's suggested that this feature is a less compact and older spiral arm, similar to the Northerm Spiral Arm, but with a more gradual curvature. By examining the Cloud's distribution, researchers conclude that its mass is approximately 5.8 x 10^6 solar masses. The analysis presents a revised explanation for the Cloud's placement and structure, resolving long-standing issues.

The objective of most optimization strategies is to find the best solution, but some algorithms aim to generate a range of suitable solutions.  In the case of complex problems without a straightforward global optimum, multiple high-quality solutions can provide valuable insights.  This research investigates whether an optimization algorithm can effectively produce a diverse set of solutions by analyzing various measures of variety in multi-solution optimization.  The study compares different diversity-promoting techniques and their combinations on a range of benchmark functions, examining their impact on both optimization quality and solution diversity.  Remarkably, the best results were observed from an straightforward, non-complex approach that employs global benchmark function to diversity management, which facilitated the discovery of a large number of solutions (up to 200) for specific functions.

We're examining a three-dimensional stable housemate problem where each agent has unique, additive preferences across three resource types and a unique ranking system. Our findings indicate that in an scenario with four agents, there often isn't a stable distribution, but when there are five or more agents, a stable distribution almost always exists. We also discovered that when all agents have the same level of preference intensity, a stable distribution is guaranteed to exist. To understand the complexity of these distributions, we created a three-dimensional stable housemate achievement function and, through a straightforward proof, demonstrated that it satisfies the basic properties of a function. We also showed that in a situation with four agents, the function is concave, but in a situation with five or more agents, the function is not necessarily concave.

A key mechanism driving valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials involves intense electron-phonon interactions, where robust intralayer vibrations generate varied valley-mixing processes, as shown through the example of hBN and mBN. This process, not previously considered in experimental studies on these materials, is significantly influenced by the distinct band structures of mBN and hBN, leading to different outcomes. In both materials, though, robust phonon-driven valley mixing occurs, creating challenges for observing the anticipated Hall effect in these materials due to extensive valley mixing during transport. This interaction also limits the functional integrity of atomic-scale devices made from these materials due to their intense electron-phonon interactions.

This research introduces the notion of cloud complexes to establish a link between Gromov-Hausdorff distances and categorical dimensions. It demonstrates that the skycomb category serves as a prototype for a broad class of examples that illustrate the various ways the skycomb structure can emerge when taking a limit regarding the categorical dimensions within a specific category. An essential property of these types of categories is that they contain a unique simple object, which allows the construction of a maximal subcategory with a simple structure. The creation of a maximal subcategory with a simple structure within a specific class of categories that have a certain level of complexity, but not the full spectrum of complexity found in skycomb categories, is achieved through a process called the formation of clouds. This process involves taking the union of all images of morphisms that apply to a specific simple object within a certain subcategory with a simple structure. These categories with a simple structure are called clouds. The formation of clouds is an important operation because it allows the compactification of the category through a process called cloud compactification, which can be seen as a refinement of the category's structure. An example of a category that arises through the process of cloud compactification is the category that represents the continuous real numbers, which can be seen as the compactified result of the category of finite sets and morphisms that preserve cardinality.

This research introduces a novel microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate within the mm-wave frequency range. The proposed antenna features a distinctive slotted microstrip topology created using the EC10, EC20, EC30, EC40, EC50, EC60, EC70, EC80, EC90, EC100 bud ecology, EC110, EC120, EC130, EC140, EC150, EC160, EC170, EC180, EC190, EC200 trapezoidal microstrip topology, which significantly enhances the bandwidth. Additionally, the unique structure facilitates broad coverage over angles, resulting in an increased signal strength. With an operational frequency of around 28 GHz and an impressive bandwidth of 14.3 GHz (3.8-17.8 GHz), this antenna meets the requirements for Wi-Fi 6e, 5G, and other similar applications. The designed antenna achieved a maximum gain of 6.7 dBi and maintained a signal strength of 0 dBi within a wide angle range of 180 degrees. The antenna dimensions measure 20 mm by 20 mm, making it suitable for integration into compact mm-wave communication devices.

As practical quantum computers approach, it becomes essential to address the issue of reliable processing in the presence of qubit errors. One potential method, the quantum reinforcement learning approach, involves employing reinforcement learning to train 'coders' that can correct various types of quantum errors without requiring a full density matrix description, thereby reducing the computational load. Our approach is broadly encompassing, allowing it to utilize various forms of quantum reinforcement learning coders without being confined to a particular methodology. Through a simulation based on a historical average, we found that these coders are capable of providing fault-tolerant quantum computing, and even improving upon traditional fault correction methods in certain scenarios.

Quantum-enhanced metrology has consistently appeared in experiments using specific two-level systems, yet it remains to be seen if this principle applies to more complex entangled states involving multiple degrees of freedom. We have investigated the quantum leap metrology in a double-cavity network using two quantum feedback control methods, the first of which preserved entanglement across the cavities, while the second method enabled rapid entanglement creation despite losses. Notably, our results showed that both methods can achieve an enhancement of log(N) improvement in precision, which is the maximum possible for entangled states with a certain number N of equally spaced points. We have also applied this approach to measure theLeap time in a cavity, with promising results indicating a substantial advantage in timing accuracy.

Research has examined direct photon-hadron correlations in Au+Au, Cu+Cu, and $d$+Au collisions at a 200 GeV collision energy to explore the emergence of a near-side jet-like structure in Au+Au collisions, while a similar signal was not observed in $d$+Au collisions. This jet-like structure is most pronounced when photons are paired with high-rapidity particles, specifically when the partner particle is within a -1.6 to -2.4 rapidity range. In Au+Au collisions, photon pair distributions in pseudorapidity and transverse momentum are uniform except for a suppression region around $z_\beta \sim 0$. Additionally, photons paired with low-rapidity and high-transverse-momentum particles exhibit enhanced alignment in pseudorapidity compared to simulations, suggesting a correlation that cannot be attributed to medium interactions. $d$+Au collisions reveal a photon pair distribution with minimal suppression and no jet-like structure. Notably, the absence of a jet-like structure in $d$+Au collisions implies that this signal in Au+Au collisions originates from interactions between high-transverse-momentum particles and the medium. Possible explanations for this interaction include the redistribution of momentum from the jet to medium particles or photons being emitted by the medium in response to the passing jet.

We explore the emulation of fermionic systems in quantum computing with any number of fermions in any number of dimensions. The hybrid digital-analog method, requiring only setting and combining of real and spin phases in qubits, is used to develop an efficient and versatile procedure for creating any fermionic state. A simplified and general approach is presented for copying complex wave functions with efficient overlap calculations, and the method is shown to support efficient determination of ground and excited states through classical computation with the ability to distinguish between them. Additionally, we outline a potential route for developing a quantum algorithm for efficiently calculating the eigenvalues of a generic Hamiltonian. To implement these processes, we describe a universal quantum circuit suitable for use in quantum analog-digital hybrid computing with any gate fidelity.

Machine learning's pursuit of optimized solutions often prioritizes performance but sacrifices reliability when models are detached from their training data.  We refer to this performance-generalization disparity as the optimization-generalization paradox.  Our work targets this issue by investigating how attribute optimization affects model generalization.  To achieve this, we have developed Wealthy, a cooperative optimization framework that balances performance and generalization by making adjustments to both model and attribute.  The Wealthy compiler enables a wide range of attribute formulations, and through a parallel search process, it identifies a subset of optimal attributes.  Our results indicate that Wealthy's cooperative model outperforms traditional methods, and by examining the nature of generalizable attributes, we have gained a deeper understanding of the optimization-generalization paradox.

Achieving intricate structures in tissue with a scale of just a few micrometers requires precise control of light exposure in the tissue over an corresponding pixel array, which our proposed framework meets by utilizing a variable gain filter and an iterative learning control scheme. The filter, which adjusts the gain of each pixel in real-time based on the current image, works in tandem with the iterative learning control to create desired structures within the tissue. The framework's non-linear feedback control allows for the rapid construction of complex patterns, even when the system has an unknown or rapidly changing behavior. This framework's capabilities were demonstrated through its successful formation of multiple intricate structures in 3D space with tissue, an area where traditional control schemes are often ineffective.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work aims to tackle the issue of developing individualized treatment guidelines that are robust to changes in the training data. To achieve this, we use a distributionally robust optimization approach and the maximum remaining entropy method within a flexible learning framework. This allows us to generalize the concept of individualized treatment rules and establish asymptotic theory for estimating the optimal treatment rules. Notably, our results demonstrate the importance of considering the marginal distribution of covariates in the limiting theory. The discussion from experts brings up additional thoughts and potential future research directions which are eagerly looked forward to.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are an attractive option for high-energy physics experiments due to their flexibility and potential for use in future projects. Researchers have examined the performance of prototype CLICTD monolithic sensors using different thick silicon substrates and p-type epitayers. Analysis of test results from the CL36e prototype involved looking at charge collection properties, signal amplitude, time, and 3D projection. While better signal-to-noise ratios were achieved with higher epitayers, epitayers greater than 3 $\mu$m resulted in reduced hit efficiency. Using a thin p-in-n prototype, researchers discovered that hit efficiency could be improved without decreasing signal quality by utilizing thinner epitayers. Additionally, using a thick p-in-n prototype, researchers demonstrated that monolithic small collection electrode CMOS sensors could operate at high fluxes, meeting invariant mass $p_t$ requirements of 1 GeV/c, which is comparable to other CMS sensor types.
