The process of incorporation, which occurs when solid particles settle into rising plumes, plays a crucial role in understanding how particles distribute themselves within water and sediment deposits. Incorporation has been found to be more efficient than other particle transport methods by up to 10 times, yet its complex behavior makes it challenging to study mathematically and computationally. To better understand incorporation, we conducted both theoretical and experimental investigations. Through a new theoretical analysis, we determined the conditions under which particles can settle into the plume, forming a distinctive ring-shaped structure. This analysis also revealed that incorporation occurs at a steady rate, which is dependent on the particles' size and the surrounding fluid's velocity. To validate our findings, we conducted two sets of experiments. The first set used a transparent column to observe the plume visually, while the second set utilized a transparent wall to facilitate high-resolution imaging of the particle settlement process. Our experimental results closely matched the predictions from our theoretical analysis.

Understanding how diseases spread within complex networks like cities or brain connections requires a more advanced model than simple graph theory, which can be accommodated through hypergraphs that capture multiple connections between nodes. Researchers have derived fundamental parameters, known as spectral and algebraic multipliers, for predicting the outcome of an epidemic in a hypergraph based on its properties and the characteristics of the disease. By analyzing these parameters, it is possible to identify a critical threshold that determines whether an epidemic will occur or not, and additional conditions can be established to determine if an epidemic will affect the entire network or just a small part of it. To calculate these parameters, researchers have created efficient algorithms for determining the properties of the disease and testing the stability of its solutions. Including the work of J. Harris and J. Lyu, researchers have derived new conditions for the stability of diseases that take into account the structure of the hypergraph and the characteristics of the disease, such as its transmission rate and the severity of its symptoms. To calculate the spectral multiplier for an epidemic in a hypergraph, researchers have developed a method for determining the properties of the disease within clusters of connected nodes and tested the stability of its solutions. By combining this approach with the techniques of linear algebra and calculus, researchers have derived new conditions for the stability of diseases that take into account the structure of the hypergraph and the characteristics of the disease, and researchers have conducted extensive tests on a variety of disease models and networks.

Recent findings on the Rashba-like spin states in the bulk magnetism of certain 2D ferromagnets remain to be thoroughly explained. We utilize a theoretical model to analyze the magnetic properties of a specific prototype ferromagnet with a hexagonal lattice structure, demonstrating how its bulk magnetic characteristics are influenced by the interplay of Rashba-like states and non-colinear magnetic arrangements that symmetry imposes. By evaluating the magnetic properties at two epitaxial growth orientations, we reveal that the Rashba-like states generate circular components in the ferromagnet's magnetization vector, thereby violating its 2D plane symmetry. We explain the origin of this violation and its association with Rashba-like states through an effective Hamiltonian that combines the effects of Rashba-like states and magnetic arrangements that symmetry imposes. We also examine the magnetic arrangements that symmetry imposes and the influence of spin-orbit interactions on the magnetic properties of the ferromagnet, as well as its bulk magnetic characteristics. We demonstrate that by adjusting the magnetization's in-plane component, the Rashba-like states can contribute significantly to the magnetic energy, thereby providing a potential method of control.

Using an advanced astrophysics simulator, we investigate how various rotation patterns affect magnetic activity in sun-like stars. Unlike the Sun, these stars exhibit distinct rotation rates near the equator and the poles, causing the stars to expand and contract. This simulation reveals that as the stars' rotational rates decrease, their magnetic activity diminishes but undergoes an unexpected shift. In some scenarios, the stars' magnetic cycles switch from decreasing to increasing. To understand the mechanisms behind this phenomenon, we analyze the internal dynamo processes that produce the stars' magnetic field. Our results suggest that when the stars' rotational rates are slow, their internal dynamos behave differently due to varying levels of turbulence and the geodesic effect, which affects the stars' angular velocity. This has significant implications for the generation of magnetic field in slowly rotating stars.

Recent advancements in Deep Multimodal Learning have led to the creation of various architectures that can handle multiple input and output modalities through distinct networks. This approach has been applied to problems such as keyword prediction in image captions and vice versa, with promising results. Nevertheless, the separate use of individual networks for different modalities may introduce inconsistencies and complications in feature learning. To address these limitations, this research introduces the K-fan multimodal deep framework, featuring a dual architecture for model design. The modular design enables the sharing of base networks across all modalities, while unique edge networks are used to handle distinct tasks. The proposed framework establishes a unified connection for feature learning and shared representations, demonstrating superior performance in keyword prediction tasks compared to current leading models.

To ensure that concurrent programs produce the correct results, their behavior with respect to synchronization and data protection needs to be accurately defined and validated. Traditional spin lock and mutex-based programs are particularly challenging to understand as their developers often intentionally create ambiguity around data access and inter-thread relationships. Ensuring that such programs meet reliability and security requirements can be complicated due to the complexity of defining thread-related properties and checking for potential violations. To address these challenges, McMini is introduced as an advanced model checker that leverages DPOR for efficient validation of multithreaded programs utilizing spin locks. McMini is designed to be flexible and adaptable to various programming paradigms, allowing for easy integration into existing toolsets. Moreover, McMini's framework enables the use of arbitrary reasoners for SMT-based property verification, mutex analysis, and data protection management. This flexibility makes McMini an efficient model checker, specifically suitable for verifying the reliability of spin lock-based multithreaded programs.

The widespread circulation of false information through social media has been exacerbated by private messaging apps, with some users directly receiving it and then disseminating it further. A recent example in India resulted in the spread of deadly anti-Muslim hate speech through WhatsApp, leading to violent attacks that killed dozens of people. As a result, WhatsApp introduced a feature that limits the number of times a message can be forwarded, but its effectiveness is uncertain. Our study uses data from an urban area in India, combining survey and phone call interviews with users, to examine the impact of these restrictions. Contrary to expectations, we found that users simply sent messages to friends and family not covered by the limits, rather than reducing the message's dissemination. Furthermore, users who supported the restrictions engaged in similar behavior, while those opposed did not use workarounds. Our findings suggest that combating misinformation may require more comprehensive solutions across various platforms.

The evolution of new species is often accompanied by the formation of species archetypes, 
from which individual organisms diverge through the process of speciation. 
One mathematical model that captures this process is the branching random walk, 
where each individual gives rise to a random number of offspring, 
whose locations are randomly dispersed according to a distribution. 
The positive correlation between an individual's distance from the origin and its offspring generation numbers can be represented by a quantity called the branching ratio. 
In this research, we investigate the prevalence of different genetic lineages within a species, 
defining lineages by their ancestral points relative to a random population, 
and derive approximate models for estimating genetic lineage frequencies. 
These estimates are based on a mixture distribution of non-negative numbers and are therefore always non-negative, 
thus preventing the estimation of negative lineage frequencies. 
In the context of the models we study, the prevalence of different genetic lineages typically takes on a spectrum, 
where frequencies are closest to the expected values from a corresponding continuous distribution, 
then gradually decrease in absolute value, eventually becoming negligible in the long term. 
The deviation of the lineage prevalence spectrum from a corresponding continuous distribution can be attributed to the existence of distinct lineage groups, 
where our research demonstrates that the prevalence of these groups typically decays according to an inverse power law, 
where the exponent depends solely on the branching ratio and a relationship involving the variance of the dispersion distribution.

The primary goal of a spoofing countermeasure system in speaker authentication is to recognize and neutralize speech impersonation through voice imitation. To achieve this, the system must be able to identify and respond to the countermeasures employed by the speaker. Standard neural network architectures typically incorporate countermeasures as additional input features, but they do not prioritize their detection. We propose an attentive activation mechanism (AAM) that allows a speaker authentication system to detect and countermeasures at the feature level, leading to improved countermeasure detection. The AAM consists of two components: an attentive mechanism that enhances the system's ability to identify countermeasures and an activation mechanism that prevents the system from learning countermeasures. The AAM has been successfully integrated into an end-to-end speaker authentication system, as demonstrated by the experiments conducted on the ASVspoof 2019 database.

We suggest a new approach to supergravity-based models of inflation by proposing locally supersymmetric simple scalar potentials, specifically with a single $D$-term, to provide a solid foundation for future supergravity model construction and offer a natural pathway to supergravity completion. Combining analytical calculations with numerical simulations, our findings demonstrate that the cosmic inflationary dynamics of these complex scalar field models closely resemble those of the chaotic inflationary models in the classical limit. Moreover, we propose an effective model of inflation based on an $N=1$ supergravity model featuring a complex linear dilaton, which serves as an excellent example of the scalar field inflationary paradigm in supergravity.

Isaac Newton's pioneering work on the green flash during a solar eclipse laid the groundwork for a century-old idea about correlated photons. This notion, sourced from Newton's citations of a paper by Halley and Huygens, has been debated among scientists for over a century. We present an analysis of Newton's findings and offer a scientific explanation for the observed phenomenon, which resolves longstanding disagreements and clarifies the mechanism behind Newton's observations of the green flash.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material defects, which often involve superconducting structures and are diffcult to detect using conventional methods. Near-field terahertz microscopy provides a more accurate inspection of quantum circuit components by offering higher resolution than conventional techniques. This study employs this approach to investigate the effects of weak links and junction capacitances on microwave resonators, utilizing a scanning terahertz microscope to do so.

We present two novel methods for partitioning the real line into countable sets of Borel intervals based on their asymptotic densities.
The first approach yields a partition where each subset consists of intervals with a unique asymptotic density.
The second method results in a partition where each subset is comprised of intervals with the same asymptotic density.
Both methods allow for the construction of distinct partitions of the real line.
The proof of our findings relies on a recent criterion for Borel sets due to Baire.
Our work addresses an open question from Kulikowski's research by providing a positive response.

This paper examines novel investment methods' potential returns by comparing them to established strategies in two different markets: one with consistent and another with volatile trends. Our analysis reveals that novel approaches excel in novel environments but struggle to outperform time-tested strategies in predictable markets. In unpredictable markets, however, novel strategies demonstrate superior results and maintain their advantage even when replicated by others. To promote the use of novel strategies, we suggest implementing client-led decision-making, where investors' goals and risk tolerance are closely matched with the inherent risk of new or traditional approaches. Our findings can contribute to ongoing discussions about the mix of new and traditional investment methods and encourage further research on the topics of risk dynamics and agent-based modeling.

Researchers have advocated for using signature-based techniques to identify malicious traffic, arguing that pattern matching is a rapid and effective method.  Despite this, some experts prefer using protocol identification over signature matching due to its adaptability and ability to identify unknown attacks.  However, both approaches have their drawbacks, particularly when it comes to evasion techniques used by attackers to bypass detection.  In this research, a new framework is developed to create adaptive protocol identification schemes using network flow data, showcasing a method that can successfully identify assault scenarios, including three crafted evasions, while a second variant is capable of detecting all nine assault cases, despite only being designed for three.  Additionally, the study reveals that a challenging condition for these identification methods to be applicable in real-world scenarios, potentially limiting their usability in such settings.

Electrostatic gating techniques have significantly advanced the study of two-dimensional materials by providing precise control over electronic properties, but their applications in three-dimensional systems have been limited due to the lack of suitable materials with insulating properties. Our research now presents a method to achieve electrostatic gating in 3D systems using superconductors, which can serve as artificially designed van der Waals boundaries. By leveraging the unique characteristics of superconductors, such as Meissner fields or Kapitza resistance, it is possible to create localized electrostatic potentials that can influence neighboring magnetic materials and demonstrate this through successful gating of a nearby spin-polarized magnetic layer in a specific setup. Our findings open the door for the control of additional degrees of freedom in 3D systems, offering opportunities in the integration of quantum modules for the development of novel devices and materials with unique properties.

A significant challenge in federated learning lies in training models across numerous devices with different datasets, a problem highlighted in this paper through a practical application - deploying customizable speech recognition with a large set of possible categories on a wide range of devices. Since each device can't have all possible categories, we explore the feasibility of training a model that can identify new categories on a client device without needing to transmit the associated data. Our approach involves several key components: first, pre-training the model using a large dataset with pseudo-labels for each category, then fine-tuning it on a subset of client devices; next, using transfer learning to adapt the model to new categories on other devices; and finally, combining the models using federated averaging. While the model is initially pre-trained, we find that novel categories can be learned without requiring the transmission of the associated data, a significant result given the inherent data privacy issues involved in speech data. Our experiments cover a wide range of novel categories, including made-up words, domain-specific terms, and different accents/domains. Notably, a direct comparison with a model that was fully trained locally on each novel category reveals that our approach yields similar results but with significantly reduced communication costs.

We are suggesting a detailed plan to create and analyze a high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state consisting of 2N entangled d-dimensional system components. The proposed method utilizes a multi-photon interference technique in an optical setup to create a high-dimensional entangled state. The accuracy of this state can be evaluated through partial projections and subsequent double-channel interference experiments. Specifically, we propose performing partial projections using both beam splitters and thin glass plates, followed by a thorough analysis of the resulting interferograms. Additionally, we are proposing a method to determine the Fock number distribution of the created state by combining partial projections with double-channel interference experiments using both single and multi-photon detection capabilities. This proposal can serve as a reliable tool for verifying the generation of high-dimensional entangled states across various quantum systems, providing a detailed framework for both creating and analyzing these complex states.

This paper introduces a novel approach to channel estimation in mimo systems enhanced by smart reflective surfaces, utilizing a hierarchical least squares method. The proposed technique treats subchannels associated with surface reflection as separate entities and applies a weighted optimization algorithm to maximize accuracy. The method is further optimized for minimal pilot signal transmission. The paper evaluates its performance through simulations and compares it to a traditional approach, revealing improved results.

This study analyzes news coverage of COVID-19 in 50 US regions from April 1 to November 30, 2020, focusing on the relationship between coverage, case rates, death rates, and audience behavior. It reveals that regional news coverage of COVID-19 varies greatly, with the Northeast receiving the most coverage. A quantitative model is developed to examine the link between news coverage and both case rates and death rates in each state. The analysis reveals that areas with higher news coverage of COVID-19 tend to have increased case rates and death rates. Additionally, there is a positive correlation between news coverage and the area's population age, COVID-19 cases, and death rates. The study further identifies four distinct phases in COVID-19 news coverage, and finds that areas with longer news coverage of COVID-19 tend to have higher death rates. It is also found that some areas with low COVID-19 case rates but high news coverage are experiencing increased case rates, suggesting a potential 'news effect' on the pandemic.

Quantifying object groups is an fundamental concept that is naturally learned by most people, however the underlying cognitive processes responsible for this skill are still not fully comprehended by scientists. We have developed a novel task called "Counting Continuous Mixtures," where a substantial number of identical objects of varying sizes are blended together in different combinations, and individuals are asked to estimate the composition of these mixtures based on a single visual presentation. This prediction challenge is particularly demanding for machine learning models as it necessitates the incorporation of both complex visual information and structural memories. We have introduced three distinct memory mechanisms - Information Loss Memory, Attention Mask Memory, and Layer Mask Memory - to address this problem, and our experimental results demonstrate that the combined effect of these two memory types significantly surpasses the performance of standard convolutional neural networks, particularly in handling larger mixture counts.

Bloom filters and variants provide efficient solutions to approximate membership queries. Despite their usefulness, existing implementations may not fully leverage modern computing resources, particularly caches. To address this gap, we present Xor Filter min and Xor Filter max, two new data structures that offer equivalent functionality to Bloom filters and Cuckoo filters. By leveraging 64-bit words, these filters can process larger datasets while reducing memory usage and processing time, particularly due to improved cache performance. We supplement this work with a cache-aware framework, CQF, allowing developers to tailor filters to meet specific requirements. Evaluations demonstrating the substantial performance gains can be found in the accompanying supplement, arxiv.org/abs/2103.01311.

This research focuses on a novel approach to solving the Brady-Mortimer conjecture, a hypothesis formulated by R. Brady and J. Mortimer to describe the maximum number of Euclidean transformations applied to a given convex polytope with at most k vertices. We begin by introducing a distinct conjecture, which is found to be equivalent to the original Brady-Mortimer hypothesis. This new conjecture, known as the "minimum surface area packing", is centered around the optimal 2-dimensional packing density of a specific set of convex polygons. 

To establish the equivalence between these conjectures, we develop certain methods and theorems, drawing from a diverse range of fields including convex geometry, Euclidean geometry, and complex analysis. Notably, we utilize theorems from the Assouad triangle inequality and Cheeger's inequality for surface area scaling. We also introduce novel methods for characterizing convex polygons with minimal packing density, which involve using Euclidean transformations and analyzing the rigidity of certain polygons to establish upper bounds. Additionally, we leverage results from combinatorial complexity theory, specifically the Sandpile metric, and the study of self-similar transformations, which informs our understanding of optimal 2-dimensional packing density.

A proposed algorithm detects an price trend indicator in a time series of transaction data, revealing both an upward or downward pattern. It uses a weighted system to evaluate indicators, producing a trend value that indicates the likelihood of each pattern. To determine the trend indicator, the algorithm analyzes the current and future prices of securities, using a study period for the algorithm's initial trends assessment. Once the trend indicator is established, the algorithm repeatedly fine-tunes its analysis with successive transaction data, adjusting its trend indicator value accordingly. A test case using random price fluctuations illustrates the algorithm's performance, while a comparative study shows that the algorithm surpasses two simpler methods in predicting price trends.

This work presents FLVoogd, a novel federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. We have developed advanced mechanisms for detecting and eliminating malicious servers and clients, and have created a framework that enables multiple servers to work together in a federated learning setup. We have theoretically proven the effectiveness of our approach and conducted thorough experiments to validate our claims, as well as provided a detailed analysis of the performance and energy consumption of our technique. We have also created a open-source implementation of our work, and are excited to continue developing it.

Achieving successful image-based navigation in real-world scenarios via autonomous vehicles poses a significant challenge due to the added complexity of real-world images. The primary issue lies in accurately replicating the complex real-world images on simulators, which typically fall short. The main obstacle is likely the failure to capture real-world surface textures. To bridge the simulation-to-reality gap in image-based navigation, we propose a novel approach that utilizes gradient information from real-world images to inform the training of sim2real models. By incorporating this technique, the transition from simulated to real-world autonomous driving becomes a solvable task. To validate our method, we conducted extensive testing and comparisons on two popular autonomous vehicle datasets, namely the CARLA benchmark and the Open Self-Driving Car Dataset. The results show that our approach outperforms existing techniques when evaluated under real-world conditions.

Deepfakes, a type of media manipulation achieved with deep learning models, have become increasingly convincing, blurring the line between reality and artificiality. The rapidly evolving techniques for producing deepfakes have raised significant concerns in various fields. Despite research on detecting deepfakes, particularly in video and imagery, the market remains understated in comparison to the threat posed by deepfake videos. To address this disparity, we introduce DeepForces, an advanced deepfake video production tool based on a novel transformer-cnn architecture, which surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in the MFAS dataset by a substantial margin. In conjunction with DeepForces, we are releasing a related CGAN dataset, a set of images, videos, and corresponding segmentation maps, aimed at fostering fair comparison among detection models, and a benchmark challenge will be announced at THUMOS/ActionSess.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets having liquid water or H$_{2}$-rich atmospheres poses a challenge to their formation histories and potential habitability. Reciprocally, these planets may conceal small amounts of other volatile components that could originate from a rocky mantle. We investigate how volatiles interact with a solid core and overlying mantle in a planet of mass similar to that of Saturn during a formation event, and observe their effect on the planet's composition and atmospheric evolution. We find that a distinguishing feature of mass-neutral differentiation is the presence of a distinctive, narrow pressure window in the deep atmosphere where the water vapour partial pressure matches that of the silicate rain equilibrium, notably the metal-silicate boundary. Such a boundary would also influence the H$_{2}$ and He partial pressures through thermal equilibrium, creating unique ratios. We use forward modeling to determine the characteristic transiting patterns associated with this 'concealed ocean' signature, comparing it with the more commonly observed'super-Earth fall-off' and'sub-Neptune rise' patterns. These distinctive ratios could be observed using a full spectrum or multiple-band photometry, and could potentially be employed to detect hidden water or H$_{2}$ reservoirs in sub-Neptune atmospheres.

In AI systems that mimic biological processes, it's crucial to develop learning algorithms that work within the constraints of real-world technology, using low voltage levels in electrical currents that neurons can process effectively. We've created a novel backpropagation algorithm for spiking neural networks that learns patterns quickly and extracts the underlying structure of complex data. This new method makes traditional neural network algorithms compatible with biological computer hardware, where data is presented as spike sequences rather than continuous signals. Unlike previous approaches, our method avoids the issue of transmitting error signals over long distances within the network, a challenge posed by the limited conductivity of biological signals. Our experiments show that this new method can learn complex patterns in large datasets with thousands of data points and extract hidden patterns in data with multiple interconnected factors.

This paper reports on the 2021 FEVAL oOL task, where participating teams evaluated model performances for predicting phrase meanings from raw text data, with results showing that combined approaches of pre-trained language models and training with weak supervision significantly improved accuracy compared to previous feval challenges. Notably, two key strategies emerged for optimal performance: utilizing detailed annotations for high-quality training data and effectively incorporating the meanings of existing words (vocabularies) to complement novel phrases. Although feval challenges have not issued a new call for participation since 2021, this report remains relevant and provides valuable insights into the oOL field.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze parametric uncertainty in problems with smooth solutions. The traditional approach for verifying the validity of these expansions relies on a posteriori estimates that divide the projected solution space into two parts: one for calculating residual error and another for estimating the error in approximating the solution. The objective of this research is to improve the reliability of these estimates by tightening the bounds, crossing verified solutions with their corresponding projections, and demonstrating that the original chaos expansions can effectively capture the original solution with minimal error. The proposed method is tested using several standardized problems as well as realistic simulations from actual projects.

This research presents an innovative adaptive approach to identifying and isolating unknown changes in data generated by a system with adjustable parameters. The goal is to locate the optimal combination of these parameters that maximizes a predetermined objective function, while navigating a challenging environment with limited information about data disturbances. To overcome this hurdle, a sequential adaptation algorithm is developed using a stochastic gradient ascent method tailored to handle partially observed data with noise. The algorithm is further enhanced to accommodate changing systems without restarting the adaptation process, using an adaptive procedure that modifies its underlying model slowly. The research provides theoretical justifications for the algorithm's convergence and effectiveness, as well as experimental results demonstrating its superiority in comparison with traditional methods from control theory and machine learning.

Let's delve into the core characteristics of dwarf galaxies through their chemical compositions and the life cycles of their stars. By analyzing a large dataset of galaxies, we've developed two main models to determine the histories of star formation and chemical composition, which are highly consistent across a wide range of galaxies. However, these models sometimes yield different results, particularly for galaxies with star formation that's been going on for a long time. To understand this discrepancy, we've come up with an envelope of possible metal circulation patterns that are all consistent with the observations, and found that the rates of mass flow through the galaxy affect the results. By using a statistical tool to determine the most likely model variations that fit the real-world data, we've found a set of parameters that describe how the galaxy's metal circulation changes over time. By applying the same method to galaxies that are thought to be on the verge of merging with a larger galaxy, we've discovered a possible sign of mass flow using the chemical compositions, even though the galaxy's metal circulation appears to be unchanged at first glance.

We define a homotopy action spectrum for a profinite group G by utilizing continuous homomorphisms to the interval [0,1] given by spectrally extended from the classical homotopy action. Establishing a homotopy action spectrum for any H-subgroup yields a convenient method for deriving a profinite group's homotopy action spectrum. Moreover, this new spectrum possesses an essential property where the inclusion of the trivial subgroup in a profinite group H leads to a profinite spectrum isomorphic to the spectrum of the integral group ring of G.

A major obstacle in creating a robust document processing pipeline lies in obtaining large datasets with accurate labels, particularly when dealing with documents that are rich in visual information. Many recent approaches attempt to address this challenge by utilizing semi-supervised or weakly supervised techniques but often require access to labeled data, even if it's limited. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel framework that efficiently uses a small number of labeled samples to produce high-performance, fully supervised models. The framework consists of two main components: Firstly, it generates codebooks from visually distinct classes using an unsupervised image processing technique, which helps to extract meaningful features from images. Secondly, it combines a small image classification network with a weakly supervised object detector, both of which are fine-tuned using the obtained features and limited labeled data. The feature extraction stage also incorporates a novel, simplified approach for extracting text-based features that outperform existing methods. The effectiveness of our approach was demonstrated in multiple experiments, such as extracting information from invoices and forms in the widely used Librisheet dataset.

The characteristics of the interface between EuS and InAs have been extensively investigated due to their potential to create a reliable spin-orbit coupling in a semiconductor for quantum computing applications. To further understand the interface, the electronic arrangements of EuS/InAs interfaces were studied in relation to various bonding configurations, utilizing a theoretical approach based on density functional theory. The results show that the electronic properties of the interface significantly depend on the chemical bonds between EuS and InAs. The study found that a covalent bond between EuS and InAs results in an optimal alignment of magnetic layers and a notable increase in Rashba antiferromagnetic coupling. Additionally, the study found that certain bonding configurations introduce interlayer spin-transfer integrals, while others do not. The study provides crucial information for optimizing the magnetic properties of the interface through precise control of chemical bonds between layers.

We propose an efficient categorization of Borel Wadge classes by introducing 
six hierarchical levels of classification, each corresponding to specific 
logical properties. This categorization is grounded in an alternative definition 
of the Borel Wadge degree, which we call $\bathe$,
and is demonstrated to be an accurate representation of the Borel hierarchy.
Furthermore, we recalculate the reciprocal limits of four key Borel Wadge classes, 
resolve two previously unresolved open questions, and confirm four more as yet 
unresolved. This study is accompanied by an interactive online tool allowing 
users to generate graphs representing relationships between Borel Wadge classes.

Deep Learning models continue to experience an explosion in model size due to increasingly complex structures like Swin Transformers and MobileNetV3. However, both over-parameterization and excessive computational burden result from this growth, causing significant inference latency and costly computational expenses. Researchers have explored the technique of pruning, which aims to reduce model size by selectively removing unessential weights. However, most pruning methods are applied at an overall network level, resulting in a failure to account for the diversity of weights within individual layers. This paper introduces ClickTrain, a novel framework that addresses pruning limitations through a focus on individual weight distributions within each layer. ClickTrain is compatible with a wide range of neural network architectures and is implemented using the Tensorflow framework. Experimental results on various image classification datasets demonstrate that ClickTrain can be paired with an optimal search algorithm to ensure both an enhanced pruning outcome and a rapid training process. Compared to the state-of-the-art pruning method, ClickTrain is capable of achieving an impressive 70.97% reduction in model size while still maintaining a high accuracy of 93.34% for the MobileNetV3 model.

We examine the full modal functionality on the distributive complete Lambek calculus (dcl). While the underlying calculus is known to have a rich model theory, our research shows that dcl with modal functions does not have a comparable sophisticated model theory. Despite initial thoughts, it cannot be based on hyperdoctrinal logic, a more complex system also by the same author, as the underlying method would fail. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a new hyperdoctrine framework by incorporating a structured approach to subobjects, which is then applied to dcl with modal functions. The resulting framework enables the development of a first-order semantics and a second-order adjoint modal logic. To test its effectiveness, we investigate the proof system's relationship with its corresponding model theory. As a result, we demonstrate the existence of a decision procedure for both the satisfiability problem and the universal reflexive satisfiability problem in dcl with modal functions.

The merger of neutron star-black hole binaries creates diverse gravitational waves based on their physical properties, which enables researchers to investigate the same region of the universe multiple times and thereby capture the final moments of massive, compact objects formed through complex astrophysical processes.  To leverage the vast amount of data these events produce, scientists need a reliable method to quickly and efficiently analyze the signals without sacrificing the intricate details needed to better understand neutron star evolution.  Although previous approaches with their inherent biases have found promising results, more robust techniques with increased computational capabilities are needed.  To address this need, we've developed a neural network model capable of identifying and categorizing neutron star-black hole binary merger simulations, which can handle a significant amount of data and provides the detailed accuracy required for in-depth astrophysical analysis.  Our model, which we call NetBBH, is trained on simulations generated by scientists using various computer programs to account for the numerous uncertainties in these events, which typically result in distinct differences in the gravitational waves they produce.  By utilizing a vast network with multiple layers, NetBBH is able to identify the binary components that create these differences and thereby distinguish between different neutron star-black hole binary types, which can further be categorized into several distinct groups.  Interestingly, during the training process, NetBBH consistently outperformed other deep learning models by accurately classifying more than 90% of the simulated events, which is nearly a 5% improvement over the best previous approach. A new discovery has been made on a gas giant planet, TOI-5542 b, which orbits a relatively cool star with a low metal content. This giant, which has a mass similar to that of Jupiter, takes approximately 11.2 days to complete one rotation. Researchers have determined that TOI-5542 b is an old planet, formed through a migration process, which has an unusual temperature around 970 K. This hot Jupiter stands out due to its lower mass for a hot Jupiter, which means it poses as a less massive object in terms of its escape velocity. This less massive characteristic makes it an even more unusual member of the metal-deficient star's planetary family.

We're examining Restricted Markov Decision Processes with constraints being linear combinations of solution values, where the weight coefficients are also restricted. To solve this, we adapt a primary-dual method from linear programming, breaking it down into sequential primary-dual steps. This approach allows us to find both the optimal policy and the minimal cost within a finite number of iterations. Moreover, the resulting dual solution can be taken as a certificate of infeasibility for the original problem in case it's unconstrained.

This study presents a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical equations without the need for real-time input from a pen input system. Unlike typical offline approaches that focus on a single word or short phrases, this method can handle full equations up to the length of a standard A4 page. It uses a combination of a specialized, highly-capable handwriting model and a novel equation parser, which was trained on a vast dataset and can robustly handle diverse mathematical notation recognition challenges. The model was trained using a dataset of 400,000 mathematical equations and demonstrated an error rate of 3.37%, yielding a high level of accuracy. The study also showcases a pen-based input system for collecting handwritten equations, which was used in conjunction with the DeepMath approach for recognizing handwritten mathematical equations.

For a supersymmetric quantum mechanics system with generic prequantum sheaf, 
we examine the expansion of complex topological vector space $H^*
\hat{K}\simeq\oplus_{i=0}*\hat{K}\otimes H^i($generic, $\mathbb{C}$). 
Here, $\hat{K}$ is the formal completion of $\mathbb{C}$ in the sense of 
formal topology, and we are considering the $i=$ 0 case. We are studying the 
$d$-closed forms that are also $\mathbb{Z}_2$-invariant and finding that 
$\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_2}H^{0,0}=\hat{K}\otimes H^{0,0}$. Here, $H^{0,0}$ 
refers to the form which is both $d$-closed and $\mathbb{Z}_2$-invariant. 
We are also finding in specific examples that $\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_2}H^{0,0} 
\neq H^{0,0}$.

This analysis examines the stability of a complex system through variability in its interaction processes. By leveraging hierarchical time series and a conditional multiscale approach, our research reveals a direct link between a network's structural intricacy and the variability of its interaction dynamics. Furthermore, our results indicate that in highly interconnected systems, the variability of lower-level interactions outweighs that of higher-level interactions. This finding is consistent across different types of interaction processes.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning has significant applications in areas such as robotics and game playing. The integration of the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) technique has been shown to significantly improve the efficiency of reinforcement learning in various settings. We have developed a novel actor-critic method that seamlessly combines HMC and actor-critic learning, leveraging the benefits of both techniques. Notably, our approach circumvents the need for backpropagation through time, which can be challenging to implement and prone to numerical instability. The efficacy of our method has been demonstrated in a diverse range of tasks, including a classic cart-pole game, and it has been shown to achieve better performance than traditional actor-critic methods as well as a recent variant that also integrated HMC techniques.

There is no prime number $p$ such that $2^{p}$ can be divided evenly by $p$. 
Assuming the prime number theorem holds, when considering the set of all integers $n$ less than $x$ that are not prime, its size is roughly $x$ times the logarithm of $x$, due to the pattern observed from the prime number theorem. 
For every prime number $q$, the number of integers less than $x$ that are multiples of $q$ is approximately $x$ over $q$, which results from dividing the interval from $0$ to $x$ into segments of size $q$. 
As a consequence, if an integer $n$ is not prime, and its prime factorization includes prime numbers $q_1, q_2...q_k$, the number of integers less than $x$ that are not prime would be roughly $x$ times the logarithm of $x$, over the product of all the prime numbers $q_1, q_2...q_k$.
